In that connection, coming as I do from that great country serviced by the Alaska highway, I think it is only right to make reference here this afternoon to "Exercise Eagle". Some criticism has been offered as to the expense of Exercise Eagle and with regard to holding that great demonstration of air power which was held within my riding at the Peace river bridge on the Alaska highway. Hon. members have today been challenged by the leader of the opposition. They have been asked if they know whether money is being well spent for the Department of National Defence throughout the country. Hon. members have been asked if, from their own experience, they can say that there has been efficiency in the expending of these huge sums of money. Coming as I do from that part of the country, I should like to say that Exercise Eagle was a tremendous spectacle. You will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, if I mention this matter because I am the only member of this committee who was present at Exercise Eagle in the middle of last summer, the summer of 1949. I saw those planes coming in from the south, the transports bearing Canadian paratroopers. Of course it was all a theoretical business of capturing the airport, taking the bridge, cutting off supplies and so forth, a field in which I do not claim to have any expert knowledge.
I saw the transports coming in from the direction of Edmonton sharply at five o'clock in the morning, over the top of the Peace river and over the bridge. I saw 160 young Canadians leap out into the air, hit the silk and come down in the course of that exercise over very tough terrain, over the top of the mighty Peace river bridge itself. Not one of the 160 young men was injured in the fall. With them came their paraphernalia and equipment. Later out of the clouds came the great transports towing gliders. These gliders were cut loose and slid down to a resting place. From the gliders great trucks, tanks, jeeps and other equipment deployed. I must say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to hon. members that it was a spectacular thing and an historic thing for Canada. All these young men who were taking part were largely volunteers who were taking up flying and aviation purely as a work of love. They had volunteered to come out and take part in that great exercise which was called Exercise Eagle. The minister must have taken the
1950	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence name from the Bible because there is a passage in Deuteronomy which reads as follows:
As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings;
These lines from Holy Writ are appropriate. So also are the verses which follow in the 32nd chapter describing as they do a land of promise such as may be found in the Peace river valley. The minister did a splendid thing in organizing this great exercise for the "young eagles" of the R.C.A.F.
I was present also at Exercise Musk-Ox because it was largely conducted through the top part of Canada and in my riding. I am sure that the military men of this country and of our allies received a great deal of information from that exercise and from Exercise Eagle and from other exercises which are conducted on the Alaska highway in northern British Columbia, the Yukon and Alaska. There they are working out a plan for the security and safety of the hemisphere upon which we live.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate most warmly, as I think most hon. members in all parts of the house do, the remarks of the hon. member for Cariboo. In reply to his question, it will be found at page 201 of the estimates this year that we are planning to spend $9,217,166 on the northwest staging route, and $7,567,283 on the northwest highway system. While these are of great military advantage to Canada, the principal user of both systems at the present time is the United States of America. The American forces, both army and air, use the highway and the staging route extensively. Therefore these constitute a substantial contribution by Canada to joint defence. There is no present intention of enlarging either operation, but we do plan to continue the replacement of temporary structures by permanent structures in accordance with the program that is already commenced.
It is a happy coincidence, Mr. Chairman, that as we are discussing the defence estimates of our country this house should be graced by the presence of one of the great soldiers of the commonwealth, Field Marshal Earl Wavell who, as a soldier, statesman and scholar, has rendered service to his own country, to the commonwealth and to the world.

I should like to comment briefly on some of the statements the minister has made in reply to remarks and criticism from this side of the house. In regard to recruiting he said on Friday last that recruits were coming in at the planned rate. If that be true I can only


say that the plan must have changed considerably over the course of the last three years; otherwise there is something wrong with the plan.
When our defence forces were first projected in 1945 we were at that time supposed to begin with a permanent force of 50,000 men in the three services. This was subsequently cut down and we were assured in 1946, as I remember, that these forces would be built up; they would be in being in a short time. During the last three years it still has not been possible to fill up the numbers of the reduced establishment which was decided upon. Therefore if it was planned that they should not be filled up before this time we should have been told about it two or three years ago and not at this time; because we were given to understand then that the numbers in all three services would be filled up just as rapidly as possible. That is what we were always given to understand.
Then there is the matter of civil defence. The minister said that the instituting of civil defence plans or projects of any kind was a matter of timing. Perhaps we can agree with that. It is a matter of timing so far as going after them on a full-scale basis is concerned. However, I do not think that the idea apparently held by the government that there is not going to be any immediate need for civilian defence plans to be put into operation -in other words, they do not envisage a war immediately-should be a reason why practically nothing is done in the matter. It seems to me that a great deal more could be done along the lines which I suggested last Friday than has been done without running the risk which the minister seemed to envisage of the civilians who take part in these plans becoming tired and losing interest in them and the whole organization going to pieces. At that time the minister said that we could improvise a plan with the information which is on hand and put it into effect in a matter of hours. If the minister thinks the matter over I believe he will want to revise that statement. I do not think it would be possible to put a plan of that sort into effect in a matter of hours, no matter how well the plan was worked out. If it is the basic idea of the minister and the department to improvise these civilian defence plans and put them into operation in a matter of hours, then they need to recast their ideas along that line.
In connection with some remarks I made to the effect that in my opinion the military organization of this country was top-heavy and there were far too many officers and men

at national defence headquarters and command headquarters and so on across the country, the minister merely had this to say: in the United States and in Great Britain they had similar difficulties. He said at page 1701 of Hansard:
However, in making comparisons with the forces of other countries, I do not think we are in any respect worse off, with regard to either the overhead or the proportion of civilians.
That is apart altogether from the point I made and which I should like to emphasize. I said that we have such a large proportion of our actual forces in these headquarters' jobs of one sort and another, and in administrative work, that we have practically no fighting forces left. To begin with, the number of fighting units is small, and up to the present they have been very badly under strength, largely because we have such a top-heavy command and administrative organization. To say that other countries have the same difficulties, and that we are no worse off as to the overhead in proportion to civilians, is not the answer. On a proportionate basis I think we are much worse off than either the United States or Great Britain. I know that the proportion of people engaged in these command and headquarters duties is not nearly as great in these other countries in relation to the total number of forces they have.
This morning the minister said there was no more information given in the United States on defence matters than is given here, despite the existence of their defence committee. I do not know on what basis he makes that statement. My personal experience has been that I get a better idea and more detailed information from reading American news magazines and other publications from that country as to the American defence set-up -the number of squadrons of aircraft in operation, and the like-than anyone can get from the questioning which goes on in the House of Commons concerning Canadian forces. Whether it is as a result of their committee, I do not know-I think it is, of course -the fact remains that merely from news sources the amount of information given in the United States is considerably greater than the amount given in this country.
The minister has said a great deal this afternoon about the reserve forces, and the number of men in training in those forces. As was pointed out this morning by the leader of the opposition, the total number of men on the roll and the total number reported as training are misleading pieces of information. The minister has had some experience with reserve force units, and I have been connected with them for many
Supply-National Defence years. We know there are always a considerable number of men who during an entire course of winter training will attend only three or four evenings. However, they are on the roll and are reported as training when they attend. I should like to know on what basis the percentages given by the minister were made up. What does training mean when applied in this way? Does it refer to the man who takes one night's training in a year, or the man who comes three or four nights; or does it mean the man who has attended on at least 80 per cent of training parades and who has gone to camp? Simply to say that 86 per cent of the men have actually been in training since the war does not convey a thing, unless we have this background information. My personal experience has been that the rolls are not made up as meticulously as one might wish.
I have one other point to mention, namely the state of training and equipment of our active force army units. This morning the minister said that the P.P.C.L.I. has equipment and training suitable for present-day fighting, and that they would be sufficient for any task envisaged. Does the minister mean by that that he considers one battalion is sufficient, so far as the army is concerned, to prevent any diversionary raid which we are told in the white paper, and have been told at other times, is the only sort of operation we would have to meet immediately at the beginning of any hostilities which might break out?
If so, let me say that I would disagree profoundly with the minister. I do not think one battalion in the whole of Canada is sufficient for that purpose. I would ask the minister if there are planes available to transport that battalion. Secondly, has the battalion the parachutes required to make landings? Does the minister consider that that one battalion, from its present headquarters, could be transported to any point in Canada at which it might be required rapidly enough to take part in a diversionary raid?

The hon. member has referred to his own remarks about top-heavy administrative staff, and referred to the fact that I had said they were similarly concerned about the same problem in the United States, Great Britain and other countries. I also said we were concerned about the problem here, and that it is one which must be watched and followed up.
I got an interesting suggestion of one way of judging-and it is only one way-just how operational a navy or air force is. The same kind of test does not apply to the army. It is to ascertain the number of hours flying or

Supply-National Defence the number of days at sea for each man on the total strength of the force, including headquarters and administrative personnel.
I am glad to be able to say that as regards the air force we are doing as many hours flying per month per man on total strength as they are in the United States, and considerably more than the Royal Air Force. We have not comparable figures for the navy, but I am informed that the same is true. The extent to which our forces are operational, when judged in terms of hours of flying or days at sea, is at least comparable with those other two countries.
So far as the army is concerned, it is of course inevitable that in a country of Canada's great extent, and with our rather complicated roles, we should have a relatively high overhead. For example the Canadian army maintains the northwest highway, and the Northwest Territories and Yukon signal services.
The geographical nature of the country, and climate, require that the Canadian army in looking after the reserve has to use a larger proportion of personnel on transport, supply and maintenance work, and the like. However, this is a serious problem and one which must be watched continuously.
The hon. member has suggested that we should do a great deal more by way of civil defence. Of course we are going to do a great deal more. But we do not believe it is the right thing to explode in all directions; we believe the right thing is to arrive at a sound plan at the federal level, discuss it at the provincial and work it out at the municipal. That process is moving on. We do not regard it as likely that an emergency will arise within the course of the next few days, weeks or months; so that my remark about being able to do something quickly should be taken only in conjunction with the fact that we do not consider the risk is great that we shall have to do something quickly. But should we have to do it, we shall be able to set up some machinery, because we have done a good deal of the early planning. From now on we are moving through the various stages I have mentioned. I was glad to hear the hon. member seemed to agree at least tentatively with the suggestion I threw out, that it might not be a good thing at this stage to get right down to the block organization.
With regard to recruiting, no one ever said or suggested that our armed forces would be brought up to strength at the stroke of a pen. We have had campaigns in order to arouse interest and they have been successful. We have got recruits at the rate we wanted them in order to keep our training establishments going at capacity. If we were


to get recruits faster than that we would have to increase our training establishments which would force us to curtail their activities when we were up to what we considered was the strength we should have at that particular time.
The hon. member referred to the establishment set-up in 1946. Adjustments have been made since then, but the ceiling for the navy, army and air force at which we are now aiming is approximately the same as the establishment set out in 1946. Of that we now have 89 per cent. We are taking some recruits for the navy, but others are being delayed, and unless the present ceilings are increased, similar situations will develop in the army and air force at some period during 1950.
If we were to get a great flood of recruits we would have to meet it as an emergency, set up new training establishments, take men out of the active forces to do the job of training and otherwise interfere with the planned progress that we are aiming at in the building up of our active force and the reserve force. When I refer to the figure of 688 per month which we are now getting as a satisfactory rate of increase for the active forces I mean that with that figure we can keep our training establishments working at capacity. On the present basis we would probably be reducing the number of people we would accept.
The hon. member asked what test was applied to training in the reserve forces. The test of training is applied by the general officer commanding the commands and the area commanders in accordance with instructions from headquarters. The tests are much stricter than they were before the war and they are such as are necessary to enable the unit to qualify for the pay which is based upon and related to the number of men under training. We have in the reserve forces at the present time 1,200 senior officers who are taking command courses. I do not think there is a reserve unit across the country that has not N.C.O. and specialist courses. That training will be extended and developed as different stages are reached, but at the present time it is being carried on on a basis which I am informed is better than what was in effect before the war. I was not in the reserve just before the war, being in it only after the great war. In my discussions with representatives of the various reserve associations they have by and large expressed themselves as being satisfied with regard to the various points I mentioned in my earlier remarks.
I was asked what I meant when I said that the P.P.C.L.I. could deal with the situation. I meant that we calculate that one battalion of the P.P.C.L.I. in the state of training

it is and equipped as it is, plus the other units in the state of training and equipped as they are, both active and reserve, would be sufficient to deal with any situation that is likely to arise at once. But of course the position will become more threatening and ominous as time goes on and therefore we shall be required to continue our training and equipping along the lines I have indicated. I did not mean for one second that the P.P.C.L.I. alone could deal with any situation.
With regard to planes to carry our men, we have a sufficient number of transport planes to enable the P.P.C.L.I. and the other airborne troops we have trained to do the job that is considered necessary at the present time. I do not say for one second that the North Stars, Dakotas and the like that we have are ideal planes for the purpose, because they certainly are not. We should like to have something like the United States C-119 Packet, but I understand that they are not in active production at the moment. We do not see that that should come first in the order of priority for the expenditure of United States funds when each plane with the spares and equipment necessary to last a year would cost close to one million dollars. The P.P.C.L.I. have the necessary parachutes.

Mr. Chairman, since I represent the constituency of Kingston City where I believe there is probably the greatest collection of military personnel in Canada-who include the R.M.C., the staff college, the defence college, the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals, headquarters for R.C.E.M.E. and the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment, which is the reserve regiment, along with other services, I think it is proper that I should say a word or two today. After the hon. member for Cariboo has given us such a vivid picture of Exercise Eagle, or our army in the air, I think someone should say a word as far as the army on the ground is concerned.
I was in Kingston a week ago when Remembrance day was celebrated. During the parade I think the active and reserve units demonstrated that they have been efficiently trained by their officers. They showed that without doubt the training of the units in that district is being looked after in the proper manner.
While Exercise Eagle was held in the constituency of Cariboo I want to mention that it was my privilege this summer to attend Exercise Puncher which was held at Petawawa camp under Major General Foulkes. It was my privilege to go there with the sixth brigade headquarters from
Supply-National Defence Kingston. Immediately on arrival at Petawawa camp we were briefed by the officer in charge and then sent out to work from the divisional level right down to the battalion level. The signals corps from Kingston had something over one hundred vehicles and well over two hundred of personnel. They handled headquarters signals from the divisional level down. The officers and men in all formations were assisted by the A.T. staff. They worked for three or four days and were on twenty-four hour duty as though they were actually in action, as many of them had been. It was not only a revival of the training which the average officer and man who had been in action in the recent war had received; but they were also instructed as to modern tactics of warfare. They were also under the guidance of very capable staff throughout the tactical scheme. Today, when the question has been put to us as to whether our money is being well spent on reserve training, I think it only fair to the department and those in charge of the summer camp at Petawawa this year that they should be complimented on their work, their intelligence and their industry in training our reserve forces.

There are one or two items generally which are troubling me. I am not setting myself up as a critic of the estimates, because in a general way I think the minister is doing a pretty good job, but in listening to the debate today I was struck by some figures that were mentioned. This morning, for instance, the leader of the opposition stated that in 1935 we spent approximately $14 million for defence. In 1948-49 we spent some $252 million, and this year as I understand our estimates are up a little more than fifty per cent. In other words, taking in the supplementary estimates and the like, I suppose we shall spend about $400 million this year.
I want to say at once that I do not know whether such an amount is too much or too little. If war is imminent I suppose it is too little; but what worries me is this. Since coming to Ottawa I have heard the Prime Minister say he does not think war is likely, at least during the life of this parliament. As the defence minister mentioned, Lord Wavell is visiting this city. Just before I came into the house I was reading a statement made by Lord Wavell several days ago, which I imagine must have shaken this parliament. Let me quote just one or two lines:
. . . Wavell said that he had been in Russia about two years in all, and he felt he knew the Russian people . . . Lord Wavell said he felt the Russians would not start a war of aggression . . .

Supply-National Defence
Then he went on to point out, as hon. members know, that he felt Germany was the threat for the future, rather than Russia. Just before coming into the house I spoke to a young airman who had just returned from taking part in the Berlin airlift, and he was of the same opinion, that perhaps we were worrying too much about Russia and not enough about Germany.
If those are the facts-and I suppose Wavell could be considered an expert-perhaps we are spending too much on defence. As I say, I do not know; but I am concerned about it. Our estimates for defence are up fifty per cent over a year ago, if I understand the position correctly. I picked up a newspaper yesterday; I do not recall which one it was. It had pictures of some jet fighters that Canada was building; but according to the newspaper report those fighters were obsolete even before they came off the assembly line. Is Canada in danger of building a lot of equipment which will be obsolete before we have any use for it? It may not be likely, but there is that possibility. I am sure the minister is keeping such a danger in mind, but I believe parliament must remember that the huge revenues we have had for the last several years may not last forever. Such a heavy defence bill could become a real burden if our revenues dropped substantially. They would be an almost impossible burden. I believe last month Britain cut its defence expenditures drastically. I am not suggesting we do the same thing at this moment, because I do not know the facts, but I believe it is something we should keep in mind.
Our defence estimates are away up this year. I wish the minister would tell us-if he knows-what we are going to do next year. Is there going to be another fifty per cent increase then? These estimates put me in a quandary, I admit quite frankly. I have no recommendations to make, but they do trouble me.

All I can say is that if you want larger active forces or more equipment, then next year the defence estimates will be larger, unless we can take the money out of defence construction or some other item of expenditure; because we are providing what forces we can with the money voted under this appropriation.
With regard to the newspaper assertion that the jet fighters we are building are obsolete, let me deny that at once. I am not an expert in aircraft production, but I am assured that the two types of jet aircraft we are working on in Canada for military purposes-the F-86 being built by Canadair Limited and the XC-100-not only are not obsolete in any sense, but are the very latest. The F-86 is the


latest plane of its type, while the XC-100, if it is successful, will be well in advance of similar developments going on in other countries. There is one sense, perhaps, in which the newspaper account may be correct. It is often said that every plane is obsolete as soon as the first one comes off the production line. That is said in this sense, that by that time there are planes on the drawing boards or at various stages of development and production which will supersede the one actually being produced. In that sense it is almost always correct to say that the pioneers, the inventors, the industrial engineers and others are working on something in advance of what we have.

I want to ask a question under these estimates concerning the new armoury in Charlottetown. For some little time we have been promised a new building there, and now that this opportunity has presented itself I should like to find out from the minister when that construction will be proceeded with.

I was there myself during the summer and saw the situation. We have moved one of the major units out of the existing armoury into what was called the gun park or the transport park, and that has relieved the congestion in the old armoury. I am also trying to arrange the transfer from the air force of some buildings which can be used by outlying companies of the various units in Prince Edward Island. In time we hope to have a new naval reserve building in Charlottetown. We need new buildings for naval reserve divisions at only three or four places across Canada, and Charlottetown is certainly one of them.

Coming from Halifax I am interested in the item which deals with fire fighting. As the minister will recall, during world war I Halifax suffered an explosion which caused the death of 1,600 persons and the destruction of a great deal of property. Again in world war II we had an explosion which caused damage running into millions of dollars. I would appreciate it if the minister would be good enough to explain this item dealing with fire fighting in order to let the house, and more particularly the people of Halifax who are interested in this matter, know what is proposed in the way of greater fire protection for that section of the country.

Fire fighting during the war and since has been done in different ways in the three services. In the air force it was found necessary to have service personnel attend to fire fighting because of the specially hazardous nature of the job they had to do in connection with crashed and burning aircraft. Similar considerations prevailed in the

case of the navy. In order to arrive at a plan that would be reasonably uniform we translated the civilian fire fighters into service personnel, enlisting the civilians wherever they were suitable. In places like Halifax, Esquimalt and so on, we have considerable quantities of equipment and trained personnel which are available to look after fires occurring to servicj ships or properties. They are also there as a reserve for civilian needs if the civilian fire fighters are not sufficient. At such places, too, the service fire fighting service is backed up by a reserve of the civilian firefighters where necessary; they work closely together.
Is the minister in a position to tell us the numbers in that establishment?
There are 274 in the naval force divided into seven naval bases. The largest number is in Halifax.
How many would there be in Halifax?
Seventy-eight are in Halifax.

Will the minister answer the question I asked a moment ago? Has the general staff consulted at all on the statement which Lord Wavell made a few days ago? Will there be any readjustment of defence efforts as a result of it? I do not know whether the minister is in a position to answer those question, but will he comment on the statement?

It is extremely difficult to answer or comment upon the statements that are made about Russia in every part of the world at almost every hour of the day. Yesterday a number of statements were made in this house about Russia. Lord Wavell is a person of great distinction who has had experience in Russia. He is not here in any official capacity but we are very glad to see him. All statements relative to Russia must be considered in the light of all other statements relative to Russia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: According to the details for this item given on page 196, it includes grants for rifle associations. Can the minister say whether, at any time in the past, a portion of that grant has been given to civilian rifle associations? Then, can he say whether such is the case now, and if it is not is consideration being given to including civilian rifle associations within the provision of that portion of the grant?

Those grants are made to the Dominion of Canada Rifle Association and the provincial rifle associations. There are a large number of civilians in those associations as well as men who have retired from the active or reserve forces. They do
Supply-National Defence excellent work. We do not make grants to associations that have no service connections. Those were discontinued a good many years ago. It was found that grants to civilian rifle associations had no service advantage whatever. The men in those associations enjoyed shooting, and no doubt improved the quality of their shooting, but when it came to meeting an emergency it was found that their particular attributes did not eliminate the necessity for military training. They might be great shots, but they still had to be trained as military shots. Consequently, it was not considered by the government of the day or by subsequent governments that there would be any military advantage in making grants to purely civilian associations. As I say, however, all the associations have a large propoi'tion of civilians in them and are definitely affiliated with military associations.

Following the question by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) about fire protection, I believe the minister will admit that fire protection, particularly in cities, has become an integral part of national defence. This fact becomes more evident as we take a greater interest in aerial warfare. If we are to be faced with atomic warfare, the matter becomes even more important.
In the civilian field, one sees in the press many references to the loss of lives and property due to deficient, insufficient or unworkable fire equipment. It is often the case that the municipality concerned was unable to afford fire fighting equipment which would have provided the necessary protection. I believe this government should place no obstacle in the way of a municipality purchasing such necessary equipment at the cheapest possible price. I do not know to what extent taxes are imposed upon the purchase of such equipment, but I do know that in reply to a question I addressed to the government on the matter I was informed that there are high tariff duties imposed on fire engines entering this country. I should like to suggest to the minister that he use his influence with the ministers of Finance and National Revenue to remove those impediments to the provision of proper equipment by all municipalities.

I do not like to be persistent, but there is one point upon which I am not clear, and I hope the minister can clear it up. It has to do with the statement by Lord Wavell. In his preliminary remarks, I believe the minister stated that the only possible enemy would be Russia-at least that is the way I understood his statement. Naturally, our expenditures would likely be made with that in mind. Yesterday Lord

Supply-National Defence Wavell, I believe the former commander-inchief of the British armies, stated that in his opinion Germany is probably still the enemy to be feared rather than Russia. I am wondering whether the general staff is studying that statement to see what merit there is in it. We might be spending millions of dollars uselessly if Lord Wavell is correct. Can the minister give us that assurance?

The Department of External Affairs and the intelligence branch of the armed forces are studying all such statements. We can see no reason for asking for less money this year because of anything we have heard.

1 should like to draw to the minister's attention the fact that we have an unusual situation in the city of London. There is a large building for the training of troops in the city of London, which is situated on the main street within two blocks of the centre of the city. There is also a naval barracks situated on one of the other main streets, approximately half a block from the centre of the city. Considerable discussion has taken place amongst the citizens of London about the fact that the government is using this valuable land for military purposes. The matter has been referred to me many times.
Has any consideration been given to removing the armoury and naval barracks from their present positions? I should like to point out to the minister that I would not like to see them moved if they were moved to a spot where the army and navy would not receive an adequate amount of publicity, which I believe is necessary for the raising of the number in our armed forces.

London is one of the places in which we feel that, in time, we should have a new naval reserve division building and that is down on the plan. I do not think it is of as high priority as some others but still it is there; and the observation that the hon. member has made will receive consideration. As to the armoury for the army, I shall be glad indeed to give consideration to the point of view expressed by the hon. member.

I was glad to hear the minister's statement of a few minutes ago in connection with what one perhaps might call the role of the P.P.C.L.I. and also the fact that they have all the parachutes which they require. I should like to make it clear that nothing I may have said in connection with the P.P.C.L.I. in particular was ever intended as any reflection upon them in any way. I have only the highest regard for the P.P.C. L.I., for their state of training, what I have

seen of it, their general morale and so forth. As a matter of fact, I am an honorary member of their mess. As I say, my relations with them are most cordial and certainly I am filled with admiration for them.
As to the matter of recruiting, the minister said that nobody ever envisaged that our national defence forces would be filled up and the recruiting required done, as he expressed it, with the stroke of a pen. I should like to remind him that a period of between three and four years cannot, by any stretch of the imagination, be looked upon as just the stroke of a pen. This has been quite a long period of time. As far as I can see, the relative numbers in the army at least have been growing extremely slowly. There has not been a great increase, from year to year, during these past three years.
The minister also said, I think at another time, that our active forces were something like 89 per cent of establishment and that the establishment is close to what the original plan was, which, as I have mentioned, was. supposed to be some 50,000 men. As I remember, some 25,000 of those 50,000 were put in the army; and as I have understood ever since, that number-the target, we might say,, for the army-has been cut down to something in the neighbourhood of approximately 18,000 and still remains there. When the-minister mentions 89 per cent, I should like to ask him if that is 89 per cent of 18,000 or 89 per cent of 25,000.

The figures are given at paragraphs 91, and following, of the statement. Perhaps I might put them on Hansard:
91.	In 1946 it was announced that the post-war establishment of the three armed services would be 51,100 officers and men. The navy was fixed at 10,000 the army at 25,000 and the air force at 16,100. In preparing the estimates at the beginning; of 1947, the target was set at 75 per cent of these figures-a total of 38,325. At that time the strength of the forces was 32,610, which included a number of officers and men enlisted for the duration only. By September 30, 1947, all the forces had been put on a permanent basis.
92.	Today the establishments for the three services total 50,359 or about the same as the 100 per cent figure announced in 1946. These establishments are changed from time to time to meet changing needs.
93.	As at September 30, 1949, the total strength of the three services was 45,159, representing 89 per cent of the present establishment and well over the target set at the beginning of 1947.
Then I deal with the navy. The hon. member for Calgary East is particularly interested in the army.
95. The Canadian army, active force, with the present establishment of 23,034, has a total strength of 19,931. At the present rate of net increase, it is expected that the army will reach its establishment by September, 1950.

Then in reply to the suggestion that the numbers are not increasing very much, there is this statement:
98. During the twelve months ending September 30, 1949, we took in a total ol 12,267 officers and men and released 4,006 by retirements, discharges, etc., leaving a net increase of 8,261. The average net increase was 688 per month.
For a country the size of Canada, I think at this time that is a respectable figure.
As to the situation with regard to the reserves, I have just asked for the position in Calgary itself and find that this year the strength of the reserve forces has increased by 17-1 per cent over last year, reflecting great credit on the units of Calgary.

Item agreed to.
Demobilization and reconversion-
250. To provide for the defence forces of the navy, army and air services, and to authorize total commitments for this purpose of $547,497,388, including authority, notwithstanding section 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, to make commitments for the current year of $401,942,006, and commitments for future years of $145,555,382, against which commitments it is estimated that actual expenditures in 1949-50 will not exceed $339,442,006.

Under this item I think the Minister of National Defence has given the example of unification perhaps to an almost exaggerated extent. Under item 250, which carries the rather extraordinary title of "Demobilization and Reconversion", the immense sum of $339,442,006 is placed under one item. That covers training, organization and administration of the navy, the army and the air force as well as all the various other items of interest, such as the northwest highway system, the northwest staging system, and the search and rescue organization of the air force. But the process by which this unification was arrived at is found in the details set forth at pages 197 to 201. When the minister was speaking on November 11, he made this statement, and I am leaving out the words which do not apply; but they do not change the meaning in any way. As reported at page 1701 of Hansard, he said:
... it would be interesting indeed to hear suggestions that . . . the relative proportion as between the three services is not correct . . . but such suggestions have not been made during this discussion, as far as I know.
I propose to deal with that subject now and to make some definite recommendations as to the proportions of the amount of money which is being spent on the various services.
Just to keep the record straight I must call the committee's attention to the fact that earlier, on November 11, I made this statement, as reported at page 1669 of Hansard:
Surely we are not putting the emphasis in the right place in providing reserves and the expansion which is so essential.
Supply-National Defence
Then I went on to say:
I suggest that if we are again to rely upon the expansion of essential forces we have to place emphasis where it is most needed in order to carry out the policy announced by the minister of meeting the enemy as far away from Canada as possible. That is not what is being done under the present policy.
No doubt it is better to discuss that policy under this particular item, but I did just want to refer to what I said on that occasion, because I went to some considerable length, I think, in pointing out that the weakness in our defence forces existed in the weakness of our Royal Canadian Air Force, and the reserves that were being made available as replacements for that particular service. I consider that the lack of R.C.A.F. reserves is the weakest point in our whole defence armour.
I intend now to try and emphasize that point and to show how we should re-allocate the amount of money which is being made available under this item for the training, organization, administration and maintenance of all the three services so that the people of Canada may get better value for the amount of money that is being spent.
Reference has been made to the so-called white paper. This morning the leader of the opposition referred to the objectives which were set for Canada. On page 11 of the white paper, paragraph 19, the following appears, which was read in part by the leader of the opposition:
The only kind of war which would involve Canada would be a war in which communism was seeking to dominate the free nations, in other words, a war in which we would be fighting for the one thing which we value more than life itself, and that is our freedom as a nation and our freedom as people.
On page 12 we find this:
Canada's services should be planned and executed so as to enable us to meet an attack upon the scale that would be likely to be made at any given time as part of a war involving the north Atlantic treaty-powers.
Such an attack could only be launched by air or sea.
Farther up the page there is this sentence:
The most likely kind of attack from outside on Canada ... in the foreseeable future would be in the form of diversionary raids.
Whether the only attack from outside Canada might be in the form of a diversionary raid is open to question. It is purely a matter of opinion, because it is a well-known principle of war that force is concentrated against the vital objective at the right time. The most powerful of all the free nations at the present time is the United States of America. If the U.S.S.R. are ever to achieve victory in the foreseeable future they must strike at the United States. The time that

Supply-National Defence they will decide to strike will be of their choosing. It may be after the war has broken out for some time; it may be after they have lured American and Canadian forces from this continent on some diversionary major operation which is being conducted in Europe; and when defences of this country have been weakened perhaps the forces of the U.S.S.R. would strike at the United States and at Canada. On the other hand, it is quite possible that they might decide to attack their strongest opponent, the strongest country of all the free nations, right at the commencement of operations, at a time that they considered opportune, when for some reason or another, without any open declaration of war, they would decide to commence operations.
It is all very well for this white paper to say, as it does on page 11:
The best way in which to achieve victory in any war is to defeat the enemy in his own land.
The Russians know that as well as we do. Are we to be the aggressor? I think not. I do not think that there is the slightest chance of this government planning a war-
Who suggested it?

I cannot see that there is much likelihood of Canada, in the early stages of a war, being able to reach a decision in the enemy's country. It is very pleasant to say, as the sentence goes on to say:
The right place to defend Canada and what Canadians believe in is as far away from Canada as possible.
That is a counsel of perfection. Of course we should like to do that. We should like to attack, as far away from Canada as possible, the enemy's forces that are attacking us. But we may not have very much to say about that unless we are going to seize the initiative at once and if the enemy has not taken the first step as an aggressor.
I should like hon. members to consider a map of the world, not the ordinary projection but a global map. If hon. members will look at a global map of the world, particularly the north part, they will see on the other side of the north pole from Canada is the whole republic of Russia. There are two clear-cut approaches across the roof of the world. On our eastern coast, coming from Murmansk over Greenland, and perhaps over Labrador and Newfoundland and on down to the great industrial cities of the eastern United States, is one direct approach. At the other end of our country there is another direct line of approach which is clearly visible to anyone who looks at the global map. One may trace the route from western Siberia, over Alaska and the Yukon and
down through northern British Columbia to the great industrial northwestern states. On those two lines of approach there are at the present time a number of undefended air bases in Canadian territory.
Reference has been made to our active force units. Of these we have five, three of which are regular infantry battalions and two reconnaissance battalions. We have been told how one of those infantry battalions has been trained as an airborne unit, and that the others are already receiving instruction in that particular type of operation.
This white paper however lays down that the role of these forces is to repel a raid. They are to be trained in Arctic warfare. I do suggest we should now place some form of active defence on those exposed air bases at Gander and Goose Bay in the east and at Whitehorse in the west, which are just invitations for any raider to come along and drop down at those points. There is no defence there at the present time. Perhaps following up behind there would be a small number of airborne troops in bombers who could land on those undefended airports. Those aircraft could refuel, and be over the great industrial centres in the east and in the west within a comparatively few hours.
Today we are flying heavy transport passenger planes across the Atlantic from Montreal to Scotland. The distance from Siberia to Whitehorse is no greater than that from Canada to Scotland; and in the foreseeable future those distances can be limited to a great extent.
I know the minister will say that Canada is an immense country, and that we have enormous spaces. I know. That makes his problem of defending this huge country an extremely difficult one. But I do suggest to you, sir, that there is only one service which can eliminate time and distance, and that is the air arm. And it is the air arm upon which we should be concentrating today in order to give a defence which is essential, and in order to prevent the possibility of these raids which the minister tells us may come as a diversion in order to carry out the very principle he has enunciated, namely that of meeting the enemy as far away from Canada as possible.
In this white paper he has said the enemy must come by air or by sea. Obviously it must. If It comes by air, and if we are to meet it before it lands its airborne troops, then it is in the air we must meet it. If the enemy is coming by sea, the situation is somewhat different. Mind you, we are told that the one war in which we might possibly become engaged would be a war against communism. We know that the U.S.S.R. have

not a strong surface navy, so there is no great likelihood of large armies being borne across the sea.
I maintain it is in the air that we have the only chance of meeting the only enemy we see far from our Canadian homes. We must take advantage of the great mobility inherent to the air arm. It can move over great spaces, and in its movement eliminate both time and space.
When I examine these estimates, when I examine this white paper, and as I listen to the minister today, I realize the emphasis is not being placed on the air force. Time and time again in answer to questions of hon. members the minister has explained how recruiting has been going on in the army. I admit that the majority of questions have been concerning the army. This only emphasizes the point, however, that members of the House of Commons do not appreciate the supreme importance of the air arm in the defence of Canada at the present time.
I would ask the committee to consider these figures, all of which I have taken from various official publications. We are told at page 24 of the white paper that the active army totals 19,931, and that it is hoped by September of next year to increase that number by another 3,000 to bring it up, as the minister has said, to the objective at which they are aiming. Then, as to the regular air force-and, mind you, please do not think that every airman is a pilot; necessarily there must be a large ground organization to maintain even a few aircraft in the air-we find the strength is 16,356; and by December of next year it is hoped another 2,000 will have been enlisted. This means that by the end of next year the air force will number somewhere around 18,000, and the army around 21,000. The emphasis is not placed on the regular air force.
Someone may say, "Well, there is not a great deal of difference between those numbers." But if an attack is made against this country and is made by air, and if we are to meet it far from our Canadian homes, then the first troops to be employed will be those of the air force. The casualties in the first few days in that force will be much greater than those in any other service. If we are to meet the enemy far from our shores we have to meet him in the air.
Let us now look at the reserve army and the auxiliary air force, and the means existing for the replacement of active personnel. As reported on page 1698 of Hansard the minister said that the reserve army had some 39,000, but we are told on page 24 of the white paper that the reserve air force has only 3,086. A total of 39,000 for the army and 45781-124
Supply-National Defence 3,086 for the air force. I submit that we are not placing the emphasis on the essential arm and that what the minister has allocated in these items is not for the best advantage in carrying out the role enunciated by the government for the defence of this country.
Then I return to the contingents in the universities where we expect to obtain the future leaders. We find that there are some 2,618 cadet officers under training in the army contingents in the universities of Canada, whereas there are only some 699 in the air force contingents. Six hundred and ninety-nine as compared with 2,618. When it comes to replacements for the essential service for the defence of Canada, we are putting emphasis in the wrong place.
Speaking before the Senate committee, as reported in the Gazette of November 15 of this year, the minister said that we were getting new men about as fast as they could be absorbed. Then he went on to say, as he has said today, that they hoped to have another 10,000 for the reserve army. We need 10,000 for the air force far more than we need 10,000 for the reserve army. If the air force is not able to absorb 10,000 men when apparently the army can, then I contend that the whole policy has been definitely wrong. This is not the fault of the individual air force personnel or the individual army personnel. We all know that they are trying to do the best they can within the prescribed limits. National defence policy is made by the government and it is national defence policy that renders the air force incapable of absorbing more men than they are at the present time. This policy must be corrected because it is definitely wrong in view of the problems which have been set out and the objectives which have been indicated in this white paper.
Why is such discrimination shown against the air force? I can only assume that it is that we are slavishly adhering to the old traditional policy which I referred to on November 11 when speaking in this chamber. As I said, this policy has stood us in good stead for the last 150 years during which time the citizen armies of Canada have been able to mobilize and train after the outbreak of a war because the forces of other countries were available to take the first shock and provide the necessary time. In those days we were able to rely on the British regular army. Are we now counting on the air force of the United States? There are air forces of the United States stationed in Greenland and in Alaska. Are we relying entirely upon them to take the first shock and to hold off the enemy who may be threatening us? Are we giving consideration to the time factor which has

Supply-National Defence changed so materially in the last 150 years? Will there be time for a leisurely mobilization of the defence forces of Canada?
I am not considering at the moment the setting up of an expeditionary force to go to the battlefields of Europe. I believe there will be time for that. As I say, apparently our policy is still based upon the traditional practices which have existed in the past, practices which were based on the concept of a Canadian expeditionary force leaving the shores of this country to go and fight and take part in the crowning victories as they have done in the last two wars.
Government policies are revealed in the estimates that are produced. Without going into too great detail and dealing only in millions and hundreds of thousands, the details of these items show that the active army is to be allocated $64,997,000 while the allocation for the air force is $44,814,000. The army reserves are allocated $8,939,000 while the air force auxiliary is allocated only $3,648,000, not half what is being spent on the army. Under university contingent training we find that $1 million is being allocated for the army and $363,000 for the air force. Again I say that emphasis is not being put in the right place.
I have been an infantry soldier most of my life and I have all the pride and tradition of marching men behind me, but I say with that background that where we are spending under these items $1 on the army we ought to be spending $3 on the air force. One dollar on the army and $3 on the air force. I have not had the advantage of discussing this matter with the committee; I have not been able to prepare details of the estimates, but those are the proportions in which the money ought to be spent. That is why I feel in duty bound at this time to oppose the whole policy underlying the maintenance of our forces, because I do not believe the people of Canada are getting the proper amount of protection in return for the money they are providing.
I am not going to criticize small details; I want to attack this policy from the broadest point of view. I ask whether the minister now has the power to change, within the item, the amount of money which has been allotted to the various services. In the old days with which I am familiar the minister was able to transfer amounts from one item to another. But I wonder whether it would be wise to grant the minister that authority, if he does not have it now, because I notice that in the estimates for 1948-49 parliament provided $2,753,192 for air reserves. I presume that in discussing those estimates we felt that was the right proportion to be
TMr. Pearkes.]

spent in order to develop the reserves of the Royal Canadian Air Force. But according to page 98 of the annual defence report I find that only $1,067,496 was actually spent on those reserves. Was the rest of that money transferred from the air force to the army? Were not the recruits brought forward? Was the training not made sufficiently attractive?
I speak with the utmost sincerity, because I do believe we are following the wrong practice at the present time. The only explanation I can imagine for the emphasis being placed elsewhere than on the air force is that we are still following the concept of sending an expeditionary force to Europe. It may be that the final decision will be reached there. It was during 1914, and the enemy hoped it would be during 1940, 1941 and 1942. But in those days the strongest of the free nations were France and Great Britain. Today the strongest of the free nations, as I have already said, is the United States. Surely our plans should be based upon the defence of our own country first of all, and I cannot believe that any other nation coming under the North Atlantic pact could consider anything different. I do suggest that the greatest contribution we could make to this North Atlantic pact, the greatest contribution we could make to what was described yesterday as the common pool to which we should contribute by the most suitable and most effective means, would be to ensure that the approaches to the great arsenal of North America were protected.
I have referred to those approaches, from European Russia over Greenland and down the eastern seaboard of this continent, and the western approach from Siberia across Yukon and northern British Columbia to the industrial areas of the Pacific. What greater contribution could we make to the success of the strategy of the United Nations than by providing a great flank guard for the protection of those industrial areas and, if necessary, the movement of American troops to the continent of Europe? In so doing we should be at the same time defending our own country. I feel that our first task must be the protection of our own country; and when at the same time we can be doing a worth-while, essential task, one that must be done under the general strategy, so much the better.
Then, of course, there are the sea approaches to this country, which are vulnerable, particularly the Pacific approaches. On the Pacific coast of Canada we have no purely service air base; we have very few service aircraft. We have nothing like the United States coastguard system for the

reporting of aircraft moving across the spaces of the Pacific, and the reporting of weather fronts as they approach. We have no aircraft carrier on the Pacific; the Magnificent is on the Atlantic. I do not know whether it is the policy of the government to provide land-based aircraft to search the ocean approaches of the Pacific, or whether it is the policy to provide an aircraft carrier to guard those approaches. At the present time we have neither aircraft nor carrier; and the cruiser Ontario, formerly stationed in the Pacific, has been turned into a training ship. That was in accordance with the recommendations of the Mainguy report, but she has not been replaced in her operational role.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have endeavoured to show this committee that I do not agree with the distribution of funds under this item. I consider it unsound and a slavish adherence to what I have described as the C.E.F. complex. Had there been a committee of the house, as has been recommended, we might have examined these problems and been able to warn the house and the country before this large amount of money was spent. What I have said today may have very little effect upon the estimates we are now considering, but the estimates for next year must be in course of preparation now; and I hope what I have said will be taken into consideration when next year's estimates are being reviewed.
I want to stress again that our first task is the defence of Canada, particularly our northern approaches and the vast air spaces over those approaches. No greater contribution could be made towards the preservation of peace than for our defences to be concentrated upon these objectives. It would be far better than making any plans for taking part in a victory parade that may be held in Europe.
Then, I come down to a few definite recommendations which really summarize what I have said. We have to have a fighter interceptor air force in being now. There must be adequate reserves provided for replacement and to provide for the expansion of that air force which must be in being now.
I entirely agree with the proposals in the minister's statement concerning radar developments. I have referred to that at every session of parliament since I have been here. I have always urged the expansion of radar as our early warning and protective system.
Then there is the question of providing active garrisons for the defence of those essential northern areas. An aircraft carrier should be provided for the Pacific area or, at any rate, ground-based reconnaissance 45781-124J
Supply-National Defence squadrons of aircraft might, if they had an effective range, perform tasks similar to those which might be carried out by carrier-based aircraft.
Lastly, we have to have protection for our great industrial centres. I feel that many of the units of the reserve army would be better engaged in concentrating upon the protection of those industrial centres around which the men live than perhaps in any other role that might be assigned to them. In the time that has been available, I probably have not been able to develop sufficiently the background which led up to these recommendations. I spoke on September 26 and on November 11, and if the minister and hon. members will read those two speeches, they will find the background to these recommendations I have made.
In dealing with this particular item, I say that if we are to provide for the essential defence of this country out of the amount of money that has been allocated, then transfers must be made from non-essential items to the one essential service which I feel must be put first if Canada is to be given any reliable form of defence. The minister has to face this matter with determination, and face it immediately. If necessary there must be not only a ruthless redistribution of these funds; but, if he finds the air force is not capable of absorbing this increased activity, then there must be a ruthless reorganization of the R.C.A.F.

Not only would we have to have a ruthless reallocation of funds as between the navy, army and air force, we would have to have a ruthless redistribution of funds as between the Canadian people, the Canadian government and the armed forces. I can tell my hon. friend just how practical his suggestions are. I would put the cost of bringing about what he has suggested at roughly around $600 million a year for a period of five years, which would be spent entirely on the air force or the air defence portions of the army. I believe it is important for us to be realistic about the problem of national defence and not say that we want this and that when we cannot get this or that because the country cannot afford it. The problems of our national defence are to find out what proportion of the national income we should spend on defence, and then see how that can be divided as between the navy, army, air force and defence research.
That is exactly what I am asking you to do.

To suggest that we should spend $3 on the air force for $1 on the army this year leads to conclusions that I must point out: My hon. friend has been most helpful

Supply-National Defence in all his remarks and in his attitude. The one thing that makes me answer him as I am doing is that I thought he went too far. I am in complete agreement as to the importance of the air force. What I do not think he did with fairness was to show how much we are already emphasizing that importance ourselves.
In making a comparison of the distribution of the defence dollar as between the army and the air force this year, the hon. member read out the figures appearing at pages 199 and 200 of the estimates concerning the expenditures on active, reserve and officer training but relative only to personnel. The hon. member omitted from that comparison what was necessary in order to see the whole picture, that is found on those pages or the adjacent pages where the amount provided for the army by way of equipment, et cetera, $63,295,349, and for the air force, $107,986,455. The total provisions for the air force and army this year in the proposed estimates of $375 million would be $124,583,872 for the army, and $142,836,365 for the air force. In other words, instead of the emphasis being on the army, as the hon. member stated, we are spending very considerably more on the air force, and that by a considerable amount. Yet, the carrying out of his suggestion, which I cannot think he was making seriously, that we should now spend $3 on the air force for every $1 on the army this year, could be done in one of two ways. We could either do it by multiplying by three the expenditures on the army, which would bring the air force expenditures to $373 milllion, and which would mean an addition to the air force expenditures of $231 million, or more than is being spent on the whole army and the whole navy today. If we were going to do that this year, we could only do it by wiping out the navy and wiping out the army.
The second way we could do it would be by giving the army one-third of the air force expenditures of $142 million. This would reduce the army expenditures by some $53 million and reduce the whole defence appropriation by that sum, or it could be done by a combination of those methods. If we are going to have an appropriation of approximately $375 million, then we certainly cannot spend $3 for $1 for the air force as opposed to the army without wiping out either the army or the navy, or else cutting them all to the bone. That shows how practical this suggestion is. But on the other hand, leaving that aside, with a great part of what the hon. member said I am in complete agreement and I am much obliged to him for his helpful remarks.
As to the importance of the air force in Canada, we have no doubt whatever. Other-
[Mr. Claxton.l
wise out of the defence dollar this year we would not be spending 38-8 per cent as opposed to 33 [DOT] 1 per cent on the army whereas in 1948-49 we were spending 37-7 per cent on the army and 32-3 per cent on the air force. In other words, in a single year we have reversed the loading and put it in favour of the air force; that is an indication not of a backward way of thinking but of a forward way of thinking such as the hon. member wants us to adopt.
It is not forward enough.

He says it is not forward enough. Again, in this connection it is important that we should recognize the need not only for the right emphasis but also for some balance. May I read a passage from a speech by General Bradley. He said:
When I speak of balance, I don't mean the dividing of funds equally among three services, nor do I mean an equation of so many ships equal so many soldiers equal so many air groups, to create a pattern on a chart. When I speak of balance, I mean effective forces equal to the tasks that modem warfare may thrust upon us. And in striking this balance we must include that which can be reliably contributed by our allies. We can upset this equilibrium by committing ourselves, not strategically, nor numerically, but financially, to plans which on the surface seem proper, but tomorrow tower over us in burdensome upkeep.
There are a good many morals to be drawn from that statement. One is this. Our present plan of equipment for the air force includes purchasing one hundred F-86A's with their necessary arms and equipment, going into production on the XC-100 and doing the other work, which we regard as essential, to maintaining the air force equipment at present levels, improving it, and bringing about modifications in existing equipment, lengthening runways, the construction of buildings for operational purposes, for interceptor stations, for personnel because we have to construct buildings for every group of men we now take on. If you take our present plans and project them into the future, we are going to get a relationship between the air force and the army which will certainly please the hon. gentleman; and that has been the course of defence planning over the last several years. But it is not going to be three to one yet and it is not going to be done without either making important curtailments in other parts of the defence program as it is today or else obtaining substantial additions to the defence appropriations. Again may I say that this work is not done by mirrors; it is only done with money. As I have pointed out, and as the white paper points out, it requires large sums of money.

In this speech, which was to congress, General Bradley goes on to say:
Budgetwise, you will note that the 1950 funds recommended to the congress provide the following division of our defence dollar for the three services. The army, allotted 33-6 cents of the security dollar, has been steadily rebuilding, while carrying on the occupation duties to which it is assigned. The air force, given 34 cents of the defence dollar, has progressed steadily in size and ability, and the navy, allotted 32-4 cents of the defence dollar, stands second to none in the world.
As hon. members can see, in the United States the authorities happen to have arrived at a division of the defence dollar which is almost equal as between the three services; and General Bradley hastens to add:
It so happens that approximately one-third of our money has been allotted to each service, but I consider this as only a coincidence, and may not necessarily hold as we continue to evaluate the capabilities of the only aggressor in sight, and future developments in warfare. Certainly any material change in this proportionate division of the defence dollar would be made only after careful and complete consideration and analysis of the roles and missions of all the services.
In other words, speaking in October, he does not indicate any definite plan for changing the allocation of the defence dollar in the United States. Here in Canada we have been changing the emphasis during the last three years, and our change is reflected by our spending on the air force 38-8 per cent out of the defence dollar whereas in the United States the percentage is only 34. Hence, far from our living in the backward looking state to which my hon. friend has referred, we are endeavouring to use the money that is allotted in the way which will best meet the needs of Canada in the order of priorities that are established.
We are not going to meet all the needs, and I hope no member of parliament has any idea that we are. No country of 13 million people with 3J million square miles of territory can do that in this kind of a world. But we can play our part with our allies, and we mean to play a reasonable, sensible, fair part and to make our contribution much in the way suggested by the hon. gentleman. But we cannot do it all at once, and I am afraid that we cannot do everything of that character without cutting into the existing program for the other services or else having much more substantial sums of money. That is what we are face to face with in this allocation.
However, once again may I say that I am grateful to my hon. friend and I apologize to him for not having referred, before I sat down, to this part of his speech which he made on November 11. I had mislaid my notes; and besides that, sufficient time would not have remained for me to do so.
Supply-National Defence
Is it not true that much of this expensive air equipment, at the rate of present development, would be practically obsolete before it could be delivered?

That is a possibility. But when we get to equipment of the type of anti-aircraft guns, at $600 thousand for each gun-completely equipped and installed of course-then I would say that we, with our defence appropriation, cannot afford many. We have one. We have it for the purposes of training, development and experimentation. No country in the world has many either. But that does not mean that it is not the best weapon there is in the world; probably it is. But it may become obsolete by the further development, perfection and use of rockets and guided missiles. How soon that will come we do not know. If it does come it will render types of anti-aircraft weapons of this kind obsolete in part. Therefore the question asked by the hon. member is a difficult one. It is one that must be related to the particular weapon, to our knowledge of what other countries are doing, and to our resources. Certainly, had we gone into the production of earlier types of aircraft than the F-86 or the XC-100, they would have been out of date before the first order would have been fully delivered. In these two we believe we have something which is up to date and which will take care of our needs for a good many years to come.

Mr. Chairman, on November 2, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Nanaimo, the Minister of National Defence, after tabling the Mainguy report, promised to give us a full statement and to tell us what steps his department had taken to implement the specific recommendations of the report. Can the minister make the statement now and tell us what steps have been taken?

I shall be glad to do that, Mr. Chairman. It would I think be most convenient if I referred to the recommendations of the Mainguy report by their numbers as given in the report. There are some forty recommendations in all, and if I may I shall deal with them in a summary way. 1, Manpower and material stretched too far. That is agreed to and has been acted on already. 2, Necessity for training ships. That was in effect before the report was handed down.
May I ask a supplementary question? How many training ships have we now?

Every ship is a training ship, but we have now specially set aside as training ships seven, including the Ontario.
1964	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
What is the type of the other ships?

Destroyers and frigates. Then we have recommendation No. 3 with regard to the type of recruiting. I differ with the report in its finding on this. I feel that the recruiting advertising was of a desirable character. It got the men and the rate of releases has not been at all bad. Anyway, there is room for doubt over that and we are carrying into effect the other recommendations with regard to recruiting made by the committee.
Recommendation No. 4, Communal entry. We are willing to consider that but do not believe that it is appropriate to a navy the size of the Canadian navy, when we are up to strength in men, and must be even more selective from now on. Therefore, while this recommendation will be considered, it is not thought to be particularly applicable to meet the needs of the Canadian navy at the present time. 5, New entry training. Recommendation 5 (a) deals with kit shortages. That has been acted upon and corrected. 5 (b) touches on naval traditions. That has been acted upon. 5 (c) deals with improvement of living conditions. That has been acted upon. It is a matter of great regret that the members of the commission of inquiry did not visit H.M.C.S. Cornwallis before they made their report. Had they done so I feel certain that a good many of the recommendations contained in recommendation No. 5 would have been treated by them in the recognition that they were no longer applicable in view of the fact that from May 1, 1949, all new entry training has been done at H.M.C.S. Cornwallis at Annapolis. That is a fine naval establishment. I have seen it. It has good amenities and arrangements, good living conditions, and is in every way suitable for the job. The morale of the place is excellent. I have talked to the officers and men and have found them in good health and spirits. Therefore it is regrettable that the commission did not go there. The reason that they did not was that, at the time the commission was in the maritime provinces and in Halifax, Cornwallis was just getting under way, and there was not much for them to see. However, Admiral Mainguy, a member of the commission, was familiar with the scene there and no doubt reported it to them.
With regard to 5 (d), a booklet on new entries, that is in course of preparation.
What is the average number of new entries at Cornwallis?

The present course is twenty-one weeks, and they take in seventy-four men every two weeks.


The next recommendation is 5 (e), training officers. That is agreed to and has been acted upon. 5 (f) deals with the divisional system. That is corrected and has been acted upon. 5 (g) deals with welfare committees. That is agreed to and has been acted upon. 5 (h) refers to leave for new entries after their training. That has been acted upon. Indeed all of these: 5 (a), 5 (b), 5 (c), 5 (e), 5 (g) and 5 (h) were mostly carried out before the report was handed down.
In recommendation No. 6 the committee suggests that we should lengthen the period of training at Royal Roads. I have always been in favour of that and that will be done. It was to find out whether or not it was in the opinion of the inquiry desirable that I put a question expressly to them. On the training of officers they say: "That practical and theoretical work be more closely integrated than they are at present". We have a committee working on the consideration of that. Then they go on to say:
That the training at Royal Roads should be followed by experience on Canadian training ships and that if Canadian ships are not available, a partial diversion to American ships should be considered.
We do not agree with the recommendation that there be a diversion to American ships at this stage. We cannot see that there would be any advantage whatever in that at that stage-that is, the stage of undergraduate training of an executive officer-to go to sea. There would be no more advantage in sending him to American ships than to British ships. We see disadvantages in both. We want to have them trained in Canadian ships. That, again, is going to cost a lot of money. However, it will be carried out just as soon as suitable arrangements can be made. With regard to men on advance training in British ships and in American ships, we are all for it, but at the later stage after the officer has been fully qualified as a Canadian under a Canadian training system.
