Then the fourth paragraph suggests that Canadian officer entries should begin their practical duties as commanding officers with a background of experience and education not inferior in quality, narrower in experience or shorter in time than the training which has been given British and United States officers.
Of course I am in favour of that. And that was already in effect for all officers training in the Canadian forces of the navy, army and air force, except for two groups, namely executive officers in the navy and engineering officers in the navy, both of whom stopped their tuition at Royal Roads or R.M.C. at the end of two years and went to England for

subsequent training. I think it will probably take some time for engineering officers to be trained in Canada because we have not got an equivalent system of training those officers here. Until that is developed we will carry on with the present system. But with regard to executive officers, I would like to see the commission's recommendation implemented at once.
Then, with regard to 6A, training of chiefs and petty officers: This has already been acted upon. It was acted upon before the report was made, and the new course was already in existence.
With regard to No. 7, change to civilian clothes on going ashore: That is something we have always been in favour of, but it is exceedingly difficult in view of the limited accommodation on small ships which largely comprise the Canadian navy. There is no storage accommodation for civilian clothes on the ships. However, that is under consideration.
No. 8, Canadian naval service benevolent trust fund: Here, as I understand it, the recommendation is that the officers and men should have compulsorily deducted from the profits of the canteen and paid into the fund a certain proportion. Officers of the navy regard that as impracticable, canteen profits being at the disposal of the men who make them, and I agree with them.
With regard to No. 9, confidential reports on officers and men: First, with regard to officers; that was already in effect before the report was made. Secondly, with regard to men; that is agreed to, and is being acted upon.
Then, with regard to No. 10, the desirability of having a laundry established at Esquimalt; this is desirable. It is a question of priority in building. Before we have a big laundry it may be desirable to have a barracks block. Whether or not that is so, I do not know. However this is receiving consideration. The need is recognized and it will be acted upon just as soon as funds are available.
Then, No. 11, living conditions in ships: That is in process of being improved. We already have under reconstruction H.M.C.S. Sioux, one of the destroyers. It is being completely reconstructed along the lines of American-type quarters, with separate living and eating quarters. We have also made a great many minor changes in the other ships to improve living conditions. There is a program established under which this is being proceeded with.
With regard to No. 12, barrack and married quarters:	We are pressing on with the construction of barracks and married quarters just as fast as we can. This year, as I have
Supply-National Defence indicated before, we have available for construction some $90 million. There is $40 million in the department, and even more than that with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We may not be able to spend all that because of the difficulty of getting the jobs under way. However, we have started on barrack accommodation at Halifax, and barrack accommodation at Esquimalt is high on the list. We are building married quarters as fast as we can get the land and services at Halifax, Dartmouth and Esquimalt.
With regard to No. 13, administration generally: We are in agreement with the report, and are working it out.
With regard to No. 14, the desirability of announcing policy; we agree with it completely, and that has been acted upon.
No. 15, liquor on board ship: The inquiry does not give any formal answer, but they recommend that the question be looked at. We are going to look at the question. It is not an easy one.
No. 16, kit upkeep allowance:	The army
and air force have plans different from the navy. It has been suggested to the navy that they should place their arrangements on the same basis. That is under consideration.
No. 17, free transportation: that has been provided in part since I came to this office, and we have had it under consideration since. It would involve a very considerable amount of money, and also would require similar treatment for the other forces. However, that is something of which I personally am in favour, and it is under consideration.
No. 18, medical care for dependents: that is done now, not as a matter of right but as a service at isolated centres. We doubt very much whether it could be widely extended in Halifax, Esquimalt or Ottawa because in those centres there are existing hospital, medical and dental services provided through civilian sources. However, in this field we are giving more medical service all the time in the armed forces to more people. This will receive consideration.
With regard to No. 19, dependents' allowance: It is suggested that the allowance be paid in respect of dependents in addition to the wife. We do not regard this as practicable or in accordance with general government policy.
No. 20, pay for good conduct badges: That is under consideration.
No. 21, responsibility allowance: That is also under consideration.
No. 22, welfare committees: The rule was in effect before the report was issued. The report, however, in drawing attention to this
1966	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence very important question will reinforce the orders which have been repeatedly given that welfare committees work, and the naval officers and myself will see to it that they do work.
No. 23, ship's routine: That is completely agreed with and acted upon.
No. 24, officer-man relationships: This is a complicated question. You cannot deal with it by passing rules. But with the general line of the report I think most people familiar with the Canadian scene would be in substantial agreement. We are going to work toward its fulfilment, but that will be a continuing process taking a good deal of time.
No. 25, training in "the humanities": That is already in effect.
No. 26, Canada badges: That will be carried out either in the form of shoulder badges or by some other definitely recognizable indication that the officers and men of the Royal Canadian Navy are Canadians. We are now at work in devising the precise form of badge that will be used.
Is the department going to take any particular steps toward the Canadianiza-tion of the Canadian navy, or is this the only step in contemplation?

The most important step that could be taken would be to ensure that all the officers in the Canadian navy receive training to qualify them as officers in Canada where they are exposed to Canadian conditions and Canadian environment. And we are going to do that just as rapidly as possible. I think it will be done with regard to all. It is in effect now with regard to all groups except executive officers and engineering officers for the last period of their training, and we will see that it is done for them just as soon as possible. I would point out that at the time the incidents occurred on the naval vessels there were no products of the tri-service plan of education, which is now in effect at Royal Roads and R.M.C., on active service.
At what date was the order issued to recall the Canada badges from use by naval personnel?

I have not that, but I can give the hon. gentleman the date when the order was issued that the maple leaf be not painted on the ships-that was June 15, 1946. When it was drawn to my attention I at once gave orders that it be countermanded. That was done before the committee was set up.
The question of income tax involves matters which have to do with the general rule that all personnel should be charged income tax


in respect of pay and on allowances that are similar to pay. Personally I have always felt that this matter should receive consideration and it has been actively considered over a considerable period. The report will accelerate this consideration.
With regard to recreational facilities afloat, there is complete agreement as to the desirability of improving these. There have been considerable improvements and we will continue that process. With regard to recreational facilities ashore, after having seen those at Halifax I believe them to be second to none in the country. Those at Esquimalt need improvement, but a new major building should come second in priority to a new barracks building. However, we should make improvements in the meantime.
With regard to films at sea, this is a matter dealt with by committees of the men. There is an inter-service film committee and a naval film society. More will be done in that field. What happened was that the choice was left to the officers and men on each ship. They pay for the films themselves. We think we should do more in the way of making educational, documentary and similar films available and also making it easier for them to rent current films. This is under consideration.
If I may summarize, twelve of the recommendations were mostly in effect before the report, four have been acted upon, eleven are in process, ten are under consideration and three are not considered presently practical.
The minister paid a visit to Charlottetown last summer and I should like to ask him what is the situation with regard to the naval barracks there?

I mentioned this before, but I shall repeat it. We now rent a building from the provincial government but it is not considered to be entirely satisfactory. The provincial government want it back and we would like to build or buy suitable accommodation for the naval reserve division in Charlottetown. I think there are four places across Canada where we shall have to lease or build accommodation for the naval reserve divisions, and that will be done just as soon as priorities permit. There are 21 naval reserve divisions across Caanda, 17 of which have entirely satisfactory accommodation.
Is it intended to have a naval division located at Three Rivers?

That has been considered and it will continue to receive consideration. If there is real assurance of definite support we would have to give that matter sympathetic consideration.

I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
The house resumed from Friday, November 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Maybank for the second reading of Bill No. 66, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company.

Mr. Speaker, when we were considering this matter a week ago I had almost finished explaining why I felt it would be in the interests of British Columbia if this gas line could be routed through that province rather than through the United States. I based my argument on the fact that the distance would be shorter; that this gas would become more readily available to the towns and villages in the southern part of British Columbia and the great metropolitan area of Vancouver and New Westminster, and that the increased prosperity which would result from the line going through British Columbia would be reflected in my own constituency on Vancouver island.
At the present time we have developing in British Columbia a situation that is causing some organizations a degree of anxiety, in that employment is not as readily available as it has been in the past or as it is desired it should be; and the construction of a pipe line through the southern portion of the province would provide a great deal of employment for our people. It would provide our mills with a market for their products. It would mean that a number of construction gangs would be operating in that part of the country, which would give employment to the men in the gangs themselves and provide a market for the farmers supplying them with produce.
Alberta Natural Gas Company
I do sincerely hope that due consideration will be given these factors. As I said, a serious situation is developing in British Columbia because of the decrease in the jobs available for the very large number of people who have moved to our province in the last two years. Any big construction project that will provide employment will be beneficial, and the net result of bringing and distributing gas to those towns in southern British Columbia will be an increase in the general prosperity of an area which is a long way from the main markets. Now that other markets upon which that part of the country has depended so much in years gone by have been lost, or have decreased, we certainly require other outlets for our goods. Only today in the newspapers we saw that Great Britain is going to purchase her poultry supplies elsewhere. British Columbia is a great poultry area, and of course if the poultrymen could obtain cheap gas for use in their incubators and that sort of thing they would be enabled to raise their product more cheaply and supply it at lower cost.
For all these reasons I hope due consideration will be given the advantages of routing this pipe line through British Columbia rather than through the United States, thus giving the benefits to our own people rather than to the competitors of our dairymen, fruit growers, vegetable producers, and so on.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to enter this debate, even though members from British Columbia should be more interested than any others. However, the other day I noticed a dispatch in the Vancouver Sun which said:
There was protest again at the filibuster on debate to incorporate the Alberta Natural Gas Company, which hopes to pipe natural gas from Alberta to British Columbia and the northwestern United States.
Then it goes on to say that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) had asked for fair play in this debate. After reading that, after listening to hon. members debate the matter, and after hearing a minister of the crown take part in the discussion, I determined to find out something about it, not only to satisfy my own curiosity but perhaps for the good of my own riding. I thought perhaps there was some difference between the bills which were presented to this house last session and the present bill. So I looked up Hansard for April 29, 1949, and found that the debate was somewhat less than intense. Hansard says, under the heading "Private Bills":

speakeroldname: Mr. G. A. Cruickshank (Fraser Valley) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 240 to incorporate Westcoast Transmission Company Limited.

Alberta Natural Gas Company

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
I found also that there were three other bills of the same kind dealt with at the same time and in the same way. So I thought perhaps the bills which had been presented by some of these paragons of reliability we have heard about might be a little different from the one now under discussion. So I looked up the statutes of 1949; and chapter 37, section 6(a) reads:
Within the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia or outside Canada construct-etc.
Evidently, therefore, the other pipe lines are no different from this one. They had been incorporated with the idea of constructing a pipe line outside Canada. I thought, too, that the incorporated companies went to the board of transport commissioners-so mention must have been made in the bill of the fact that the company proposed to build entirely within the dominion of Canada or within the province of British Columbia.
With respect to the Westcoast Transmission Company, I find the following information: Their bill was presented to this house in April, 1949, and the company was duly incorporated. On May 10, they filed an application with the board of transport commissioners pursuant to the Pipe Lines Act. On May 11, they filed a second application to build through Kingsgate, on practically the same route as that proposed by the company in this bill with which we are now dealing. On October 13, 1949, Westcoast filed an application for a new route through Kamloops and the Hope-Princeton highway. On November 15, 1949, the company withdrew its original application to build an all-Canadian route, leaving the application before the board for the route through Kamloops and the Hope-Princeton highway. Whichever company receives a charter, we hope that is the route that will be built.
May I reflect, sir, the feeling expressed by the member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) when he spoke of fair play for this company. As a new member, perhaps I should be careful about what I say because hon. gentlemen who have been here much longer than I know better than I how the business of this house should be conducted. I do not concede that the gentlemen who have been in this house longer than I know more about the spirit of fair play and understanding. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these people should be allowed, as were those who presented bills during the last session, the right to have the bill stand on its own merits before a committee. Then the particulars of this company could be discussed.

May I say that I am getting my information from exactly the same place as other hon. members who have mentioned some of the details regarding this company. The company has not presented one location for its pipe line, but has presented five different locations. They will tell the committee and the board of transport commissioners that those five routes will have to stand on their own merits. It is easy to understand that if a pipe line is built through the United States, as has been mentioned in this house, it is the cheap route from both a construction and a maintenance point of view. As a result, the natural gas which arrives in Vancouver will cost less. The company will say, too, that it has four other lines, each of which will cost more to construct and maintain. Depending upon which of the five routes is chosen, the gas will cost a different price in the lower mainland of British Columbia. That is the way it should be; that is what the other companies are doing and should do.
Anyone living on the west coast must understand the pipe line will cost something like $200 million, and that gas cannot be profitably sent into that part of the country with its small population, without the surplus being exported to the United States. It does not matter who builds that pipe line in British Columbia, the company will have to send the surplus to the United States. As a new member I believe I have the right to say to you, sir, and to the house, "Let us give this company fair play". I do not care who builds a pipe line into British Columbia. In common with my friends on the other side of the house, the hon. member for Yale and the hon. member for Kootenay West, I shall insist that an all-Canadian route be built. We will fight for that and will continue to fight for it, but that has nothing to do with giving the company mentioned in this bill fair play.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on this bill. At the outset may I assure you that before I sit down I shall endeavour as best I can to answer the charges and insinuations which were so freely dispersed in the house by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I am going to try tonight, if I can, to give the house a picture which everyone can understand as to what we are dealing with in this bill.
The natural gas which will go through this pipe line is, at the moment, produced altogether in the province of Alberta. I believe we should understand thoroughly one other fact, and that is that a capital expenditure of $125 million will be necessary. There is only a market in the western area for one pipe line; that is an economic fact which no

one with any knowledge of the matter at all can possibly deny. Now it is said, and correctly, that various interests should have an opportunity of bidding, so to speak, for that business because all of us say how much we abhor monopolistic practices. Let us remember, then, there is going to be only one pipe line built.
The next thing is that this pipe line shall be built on Canadian soil. Before I go further, perhaps I should make a personal observation. At one time, I signed one of the bills as a sponsor. I learned a good deal about the thing, and after that I asked to be relieved. The gentleman with whom I was dealing very kindly granted me that permission. I am quite sure I could have done it, but I would not have done it, of course, without their complete acquiescence. What are we dealing with? As I said a moment ago, the gas is produced almost entirely in the province of Alberta. The Pacific Petroleum Company did bring in one or two gas wells a few days ago in the Peace river section which lies within the province of British Columbia. I am anxious, sir, that the house should understand that the market will absorb 200 million or 250 million feet of gas a day, certainly in peak times. This means that in the winter when so many people are using gas, 250 million feet per day is no exaggeration. We are not talking, therefore, about one or two gas wells; we are talking about 1,500 or 2,000 gas wells. That is what will be required to take care of the market on the Pacific coast, that is both the Canadian and United States markets.
We can rule out immediately any idea of building a pipe line to supply only the city of Vancouver. It just is not possible. It would be silly to even contemplate such a venture. Of course, no one will contemplate it, let alone do it. Now then, what is the history of this gas?
Gas was first found underneath the city of Medicine Hat. On the only visit that Kipling made to western Canada, he described Medicine Hat as a city with all hell for a basement. That was about the situation at that time. There was gas there. Private people and private companies were operating and drilling gas wells right in their own yards and producing their own gas because that property, as to what is on the surface or what is underneath the surface, belongs neither to the provincial government nor to any other government.
So the gas was first used in Medicine Hat. There it is produced from the sand. To give you an idea of what that sand is like, may I say that it looks something like a rubber sponge that you might have in your bathtub;
Alberta Natural Gas Company but there is no oil in association with it. Then, in 1912, certain people who did not mind a hazard built wells in Bow Island, which is south and west of there, about midway between Medicine Hat and Lethbridge. That gas was piped to the city of Calgary and to the city of Lethbridge; and that also is what is called sweet gas. It comes from a sand similar to that which supplies the city of Medicine Hat. That gas was put into operation in Calgary. A distribution system had to be built, of course, but it was put in there in the year 1912. Supplies ran dangerously short, and about the year 1921, I think it was, the Imperial Oil Company drilled in No. 4 in Turner valley. That gas, as is the oil there, is not produced from a sand. It is produced from a limestone called the Madison limestone. In appearance it looks about as solid a piece of rock as you could get. While you cannot compress a liquid, you can compress gas; and nature compresses it to a state where it is roughly under a pressure of two thousand pounds to the square inch. The later discoveries, all those discoveries in the north and centering on the great and beautiful city of Edmonton, are found in what we call the Devonian limestone which is a later stratification of rock in the earth's surface. We must remember that many things happened long before you, sir,-and I say this with respect- were Speaker of the House of Commons. Nature has been operating for a long time. The Madison limestone, from which we get gas in Calgary at 6,000, 7,000, 10,000 and 12,000 feet, is the same limestone which is exposed away up in the air in those mountains which surround the town of Banff. It is the same strata, but with the tremendous heat generated in the earth sometimes these strata were thrown up high in the air-very high indeed. That is the Madison. They are getting it now, as I say, at a mile-and I think there are 5,280 feet in a mile-from the Devonian, which is a much lower stratification of limestone than is this Madison.
I mention these things for this reason. I wish to say and to lay it down as a basic proposition that gas piped in a pipe line is an entirely different matter from crude oil. Crude oil must go through a refinery before it is good for man for any purpose whatever. On the other hand, gas is power, and power which can be used; the minute you bore a hole through a pipe line containing it that gas can be used for many different purposes, and can be used immediately without preparation.
For example, just outside the city of Calgary we have an ammonia plant that was built by the dominion government. In that

Alberta Natural Gas Company ammonia plant, in producing ammonia, which is one of the chief factors for explosives which were used all over Canada and all over the United States during the war, the gas is not used for heating purposes. The ammonia is extracted from that natural gas as it comes into that plant; and it is now being used to produce fertilizer which is today being sold clear down on the gulf coast in the United States. I say this in an endeavour to impress upon this house just what a particularly useful item this product is.
Much has been said about the route of this pipe line. In the notice of one of these lines now before the house, the applicants were extremely frank indeed. Under our law you must give a notice that you are applying for a private bill. This group say that they are going to begin at a point at or near Calgary, go down through the Crowsnest pass to Kings-gate and thence into the United States. My position will finally be, and I will begin with it now, that I am opposed to the incorporation of any company unless in that incorporation which is now being sought in this House of Commons that route shall be set out on Canadian soil. That does not leave tremendous differences between us, because the sponsor of the bill has said that this particular company, the Alberta Natural Gas Company, has five lines to the Pacific coast, ending in Vancouver. Those five lines are marks on a map and nothing else, Mr. Speaker. I could draw ten without any difficulty, and I do not know anything about surveying.
The point I intend to begin with and to end up with is that in this or any other bill we should have and we must have a route showing, broadly speaking, the course which this line will take. The right hon. the minister has said that it lies largely with the province of Alberta as to whether or not the export of gas from that province will be approved. He also told us-and both of these statements are quite correct-that, under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, he must give his permit for gas leaving the Dominion of Canada. He assured us, and I have no doubt that he meant every word he said, that he would see to it that Canadian consumers were taken care of first. This is not the first time since I came to the House of Commons that we have had a new Minister of Trade and Commerce. Much as we respect the right hon. gentleman who occupies the position, I think that perhaps most of us will live long enough to see another-and I hope he also will be a right hon. gentleman-sitting in his place.
The only way to protect this position is to have it in the statute. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, a railway company-and perhaps this is just as important as a railway


company-coming to this House of Commons and asking the right to build railways in the Dominion of Canada and giving nothing more in the way of detail? They would be laughed out of the House of Commons. Well, the parallel which I give you is an appropriate and very apt one.
This bill says nothing at all-in its notice the other one did tell the route it was going to take-as to the route it will take. The sponsor may tell me that if they have to they will build it through the Dominion of Canada. I have no doubt that the sponsor meant everything he said, but knowing something about sponsors of private bills in this House of Commons I think that they rather lose their authority once the bill is passed. They are not exactly the board of directors who are controlling the enterprise, whatever it may be.
The minister said that if this filibuster continued he would see to it that the government assigned days for the discussion of this particular bill. If the government want to make this a government bill let them do it. Then we shall all know where we are, because what he said means this:	"I say that
this bill is going through this house and we shall stop discussion or we shall assign hours to it so that you simply cannot talk about it any more."

On a point of order, the hon. gentleman has put words in my mouth. What I said was that hon. members were entitled to say whether this bill would pass or not, and that no small group of people were entitled to deny them that right.

May I admit that the minister is accurate in repeating what he said. I did not endeavour to repeat it word for word, but with the greatest respect and deference, the minister did by clear and plain inference indicate that this thing was going through the house willy-nilly with respect to those of us who oppose it. I am asked to read what the minister said. Let us both be accurate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do it in the same tone of voice, too.

This is what the minister said, as reported at page 1806 of Hansard:
I should like also to say a word about what seems obviously to be a filibuster in connection with these bills. The government will not permit any small number of members to prevent this house as a whole from voting on a private bill. If these bills continue to be talked out in the limited time permitted for private bills, the government will ask the house to suspend the rules and provide whatever time is required to finish the discussion and to obtain a vote on such bills.

Perhaps both of us will agree that I have correctly read what was said at that time. Let us carry this a step further. We as a house are entitled to consider private bills. What is the object of any member, particularly those who are not cabinet ministers and who perhaps have neither the opportunity nor the calibre to occupy that position, bringing in a private bill if it is to be treated by the government as a government piece of business? And that is exactly what is going on in the house now. May I add this? It might be thought by someone that I have other interests to serve. I want to correct that by this simple statement. I am prepared to vote for any gas-line bill which in the bill itself, which is the law, provides an acceptable route for the transportation of that gas. Having said that, I think I may be reprieved, or whatever the proper word may be, of the suggestion that I might have any interest in it.
The word "monopoly" is a hateful one. There is no doubt about that. But we do come to places where perhaps that is the only way that things can be done. I think of a number of government enterprises such as the Polymer Corporation in Sarnia, and some of these various things where the government itself has a monopoly. I am not quarreling with that. We may as well be realists in this business and look the facts of life straight in the face. I think something else should be done. When we as members of the House of Commons know that this market is capable of maintaining only one pipe line we should see to it in the bills themselves that there is no opportunity given to corporations, which not in this instance alone but in other instances may be brought here for incorporation by promoters with a view to selling shares to the Canadian people, that in the end result, if they are not the persons chosen to operate the pipe line, will be absolutely worthless.
These changes can be made. They can be made by the sponsors of the bill by a very simple amendment which can be easily brought in. So far as I am concerned I will not vote for any bill which has not got a Canadian t route. Why, the position is so absurd.
Remember this, Mr. Speaker: the minute a line containing gas crosses the United States border we have no control over that gas. It is controlled by the people in whose country it lies. One may readily say that if such a situation should arise we will, under the act which the minister controls, revoke the permit, and authority lies in the act for just such action if he cares to exercise it. Well, it is all right to put something down on a piece of paper, and to take another
Alberta Natural Gas Company piece of paper and sign something and say that is all off. That in effect, Mr. Speaker, kills the whole enterprise. Let us be realists again. This permission to export and to use elsewhere must continue to exist as long as there is gas to satisfy that situation. But remember, if the gas is cut off by the Americans, or they adopt some other method with respect to it, Vancouver will have been served. Vancouver, being at the tail end of the pipe line, is at the mercy of people over whom we have no practical control. That, I think, is the greatest argument for this line to be on Canadian soil.
Some people may think that in view of the attitude I took on an oil line perhaps I am being inconsistent. I did point out, and I repeat, the very great and distinct difference there is between carrying oil in a pipe line and carrying gas. I give you one illustration. In Calgary we have a plant using natural gas as its main intake product in the making of fertilizer. During the war, I think the right hon. minister will admit-and this is very much in his favour, because he built it-it was very useful. We do not quite know where the allies might have been, had it not been for the ammonia produced in the plant from which at least a very considerable portion of our explosives was made.
Probably I told the house that that plant today is shipping its product of fertilizer, with all the freight rates against it, and selling the major portion of it along the gulf coast of the United States. Let us assume for a moment that this line we are talking about went through the United States-and do not think I am talking a lot of nonsense. I know that is their scheme. I know all about it. Five lines on the map, it is true; but I have known this thing for the last eighteen months. I know where they want to go; they want to go through Kingsgate.
We hear stories about building it along the Canadian border. Did you ever take a look at the mountains they would have to carry it over along there? Even to mention the thing shows how extremely impossible, and even silly, it is. And so I come back to this, that I want to meet the objections everyone has made. I want to be relieved of any charge that I am favouring the West-coast Transmission Company, I think it is called-or some such name as that.
According to the minister-at least I draw this inference from what he said-his view was: "Let us pass this bill. Is a private bill incorporating a company to be stopped in the House of Commons?" Remember, Mr. Speaker, that this pipe lines bill was passed. Remember that up to that time anybody, any group of us from anywhere in this House of
1972	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company Commons, could go to the Secretary of State and secure incorporation of a pipe line company or any other kind of company.
So in this case parliament saw fit to say, "If you are dealing with pipe lines carrying oil and gas you must get a private bill through parliament." Otherwise anyone could get a bill and then go and make his own arrangements with respect to the land through which the pipe line passed, and so on.
It was a good act; I am all in favour of it. But it came to this parliament-and what for? It was to stop this business of simply getting a certificate from the Secretary of State that you were incorporated and ready to do business. The pipe lines bill was passed in order that this parliament could pass judgment upon it, and say whether or not it was in the interests of the dominion of Canada that such-and-such a charter be granted.
I think that completes everything I have to say, except this: We are told that if this goes through quickly it will go to a committee, and that there in that committee we may ask these people where they are going, what money they have and what the possibilities are of their carrying out the enterprise. It is there that I take straight issue with the sponsor and with the minister. If they will in their statute tell me where they are going, then I shall know how to vote. If they are going to go out of southern Alberta I will vote against it-and I don't care who the company is. But in the north the story is entirely different. There we have those great areas in Alberta and in British Columbia which will be helped -because gas is power. Power is the thing the world needs.
In our oil fields of Alberta today we are producing daily the energy of four Niagara falls. I mention that to give some idea of just what power means. This is oil, turned into gasoline and used for power. Here we have a product going through these lines which at your home, or yours, or yours, or anyone else's, can be tapped. Of course there must be some sort of reduction to bring it to your home, because you would get your gas at ounces of pressure rather than thousands of pounds. But it is there, and it is ready to be used.
And remember this, that it is utterly impossible for anyone to build a gas line without building a road-and a good one at that. Because over that road you must take heavy pipes and all the fittings and heavy equipment. Remember, this will be about a 26-inch pipe-certainly 24-inch, or more-and you


can imagine the size of that. You don't hook that on the end of your jeep, and carry it in. You have to have a road to carry it on.
It will mean more for the development of northern Alberta and northern British Columbia than any other factor of which I have yet heard, up to this particular time. And so I am not content with the assurance of anybody that so-and-so will be the situation, when in a few words the sponsor of the bill could put it in the bill. When that is done-perhaps I am hard to satisfy-then I, indeed, will be satisfied.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only two or three minutes-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That will be new.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Don't spin it out by making interruptions-to answer the well-put but I still feel only plausible argument of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode). The hon. member's plea was that we let this bill pass second reading and go to a committee.
I wish to remind him and hon. members of the house of the fact that on a good many occasions we have found to our sorrow that if there is a measure to which we are opposed and we fail to state that opposition at this stage, or if there is some provision concerning which we want positive assurance and do not get it on second reading we are sunk.
Last year one of the bills which went through the house after some debate was that concerning the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company. I cannot find that anything was even said about the route of that pipe line- not here in the house at any rate. But none of us knew then that it was going to go out of Canada, and down to Superior, Wisconsin. In other words, this is the sort of thing we are up against. Things happen after these companies are incorporated which we do not know about unless we receive the assurance at this stage-and in the bill itself, as my colleague from Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) reminds me, and as was suggested by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith).
I want to remind hon. members about another bill during the session of 1948, that concerning the Bell Telephone Company, which asked for certain rather substantial increases in capitalization. From the floor of the house we tried to get at this stage the assurance that there would not be any increase in rates. Appeals were made to us, just like the one the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has made, to let the bill go to committee, to let it have second reading, to be fair to the bill and fair to the company.

Alberta Natural Gas Company
Well, the bill went to committee and a sort of half assurance was given in committee that there would not be any increase in rates. But where are we at the present time? The Bell Telephone Company is not only before the board of transport commissioners in a general application for a substantial increase in rates, but today it filed an interim application with respect to a surcharge. If it were in order I would take time out to protest strongly against it; but I note your objection, Mr. Speaker, and you are right, it is not. So I just register my protest. My point is that examples of that kind remind us, and rightly so, of the extreme importance of the second-reading stage of a bill. It is not a stage to be passed over lightly, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has urged. It is at this stage that we must get assurances with respect to points about which we are concerned, and that is exactly what we are trying to do.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express briefly my opposition to this bill on the same grounds as I opposed the bill we were discussing the other evening, the bill to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. I am not going to take the time of the house to repeat the arguments I advanced on that occasion. I support the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and oppose this bill on the same grounds.
I want to make it quite clear that we do not make any distinction between these companies. We are opposing this bill because we believe that at least the approximate route of the pipe line should be indicated in the bill. We are opposing the bill on the principle that Canadian natural resources should be used first to serve Canadian interests and Canadian communities. Therefore, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones):
That Bill No. 66 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house further consideration of this bill should be deferred until the house has been assured that the route of any pipe line built by the proposed company will be laid out so as to serve Canadian requirements before any such pipe line leaves Canadian soil.
I move the adjournment of the debate.

The	hour for private and
public bills having expired, the house will	
revert to the business under consideration at six o'clock.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE Demobilization and reconversion-
250. To provide for the defence forces of the navy, army and air services, and to authorize total commitments for this purpose of $547,497,388, including authority, notwithstanding section 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, to make commitments for the current year of $401,942,006, and commitments for future years of $145,555,382, against which commitments it is estimated that actual expenditures in 1949-50 will not exceed $339,442,006.

I should like to ask the minister one question in connection with the form of these estimates. I remember that

Supply-National Defence in 1945 the estimates were broken down, in much the same way as the estimates of other departments, into quite a large number of items. We had the equipment item for the army as one item, the pay item, and so on.
I have been wondering how long it would be before the items in the national defence estimates would again be broken down in that way instead of practically all expenditures being put under the large heading, "demobilization and reconversion".

Certainly, the title "demobilization and reconversion" has been out of date for some time and will be dropped. Consideration will be given by the treasury officials to the point made by the hon. member for Calgary East.

Would the minister give assurance to the house that an adequate portion of the naval training is being carried out in Arctic waters? It just occurred to me that there have been several instances in which different jobs have had to be done in the Arctic, and the Department of Transport has let the contracts out to civilian contractors. Would it not be worth while training for the navy to undertake those jobs rather than let them to outsiders?

I quite agree that the greatest emphasis should be on the operation and training in Arctic waters. During the second world war the role of the Canadian navy, until the closing stages of the war, was largely anti-submarine work, convoy work and protection of coastal waters in the north Atlantic, which is not so different in many ways from the Arctic. Towards the end of the war it became necessary for us to co-operate with forces in the Pacific. We had an aircraft carrier on loan from the British admiralty, the Warrior, which was not suited for use in northern waters. It was designed for use in the more temperate zones. This ship was exchanged for the Magnificent, which is a winterized ship, and since then we have been proceeding with the adaptation of our own vessels for winter use.
Last year the first operation into Hudson bay ever conducted by the Canadian navy was undertaken. The Magnificent went up as far as Hudson strait, and two destroyers moved on into Churchill. We regard that as an essential part of a training operation. In line with that, a contract for a naval icebreaker has been let, which will also be suitable for use as a transport. When it is completed it will enable us to do much more of the job up north.

I gather the icebreaker to which you refer is a shallow draft vessel.
[Mr. Harkness.l
Yes.

Has the Department of
National Defence any idea of providing a base at Churchill at which naval vessels might effect minor repairs? At present there are no facilities in the port of Churchill for effecting even minor repairs to any vessel, and if Hudson bay is to be used at all by the navy some provision will have to be made for repairing vessels at that port.

I am afraid, sir, it would be too costly and uneconomic to provide shore-based facilities for repairing naval or merchant vessels there. Naval vessels can make considerable repairs with their own equipment and skilled personnel.

Would the minister tell us what steps have been taken for the protection of those northern airfields, such as Whitehorse, Gander, and Goose? Are there any troops located in the immediate vicinity, and if so what troops are they? How long would it take the nearest forces, which are available and earmarked for the purpose, to move to those airfields if the occasion arose?

At the moment, sir, there are virtually no troops in those locations for the protection of the places mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). At Whitehorse, there are some engineers and there is, of course, a good landing field. There are some air force personnel there. The exercise which is planned for the early part of February will be related to that problem.
There is a considerable force of air force but there are virtually no ground troops except army service corps and the like at Goose. There are small details of servicing units. There is only a small group of airforce men related to transport at Gander. There is virtually no provision yet made for the ground protection of these places. We hope that will be worked out in time, but it is not there yet.

How far has the organization of the Canadian Rangers developed in the Yukon and Northwest Territories? Can the minister give us some idea as to how that organization is equipped and how many companies have been formed?
There are a considerable number of companies and new companies are being authorized from time to time. The total authorized strength of the corps is 5,000, all ranks.

How many have been
recruited?

I have not that information. The organization of the corps is proceeding, and it is definitely related to the sort of problem the hon. member mentioned in his earlier question, though the real defence of important military establishments must of course be done by other units.
Can the minister say how the Rangers are going to be armed?
With a rifle, a bayonet, a belt and ammunition.

The minister told the member for Peterborough West that the department was receiving mechanized equipment faster than covered storage could be provided for it. Can the minister state how much equipment is in covered storage and how much is in the open?

There are approximately
20.000	motor vehicles in the armed forces, and of that number there must be approximately
6.000	in open storage at parks and mobilization centres. Then, a considerable portion of the motor vehicles issued to local units, particularly the reserve forces, are stored in the open. There is less than half, but quite a considerable proportion.
Is this new equipment?
This is largely equipment that was in Canadian hands at the end of the war and was not disposed of because it was kept for issue to the active and reserve forces or in mobilization stores.
Is none of it new equipment?

Some of it is new, yes. We purchase equipment from time to time, but the only new equipment that would be out in the open would be equipment which is regularly kept in the open such as scrapers, road-making equipment, blowers and that kind of thing.
I can give the hon. member the information he wanted about the Rangers. Nineteen companies have been organized.
Have the frigates in the Canadian navy been equipped with turbine engines? If not, has any consideration been given to doing that?

My information is that no frigates in the Canadian navy were equipped with turbine engines, although the later-type frigates were equipped with higher-speed reciprocating engines. We are not contemplating the equipping of frigates with turbine engines. What we are doing is starting the construction of a new type of anti-submarine vessel, with turbine engines. That will be a high-speed, anti-submarine vessel of considerable power and speed, and
Supply-National Defence of a new type which is being designed in Canada, largely on Canadian plans, but using adaptations of British and United States plans. Our idea is that, in order to cope with the submarines we fear an enemy might have, it would require vessels with greater speed than the frigates would have, even if equipped with turbines, and with quite different characteristics of draught, vibration and equipment.
That is what I wanted to know, Mr. Chairman, because in the latter part of the war we could not catch up to the submarines.

I was perturbed today by a short piece I read in the Financial Post which is dated November 19; apparently they are a little bit ahead of themselves in publication. I should like to ask the minister about it. It reads as follows:
When the Post began probing this situation,-
That is, the expansion of the national film board; the article is headed "Film Board Monopoly Facing Major Test?"
-it found that the Department of National Defence no longer uses the film board on "classified" (i.e. secret) work for security reasons.
As a result, films "classified" for security reasons are being placed by the Department of National Defence with outside commercial organizations.
This is actually now happening.
It is a terrific blow to N. F. B. pride and prestige; shoots the government movie monopoly full of holes so far as this department of government is concerned.
Apparently there is no chance of this policy being reversed until R.C.M.P. authorities "screen" the N.F.B. staff; declare them Okay so far as national security is concerned.
N.F.B. officials openly declare their intention of breaking through this barrier; insist that they must again be given a monopoly of national defence movie business, but there is presently no indication elsewhere in Ottawa that this policy will be changed under present conditions.
That is the end of the quotation. I should like to ask the minister if that is correct, what films are given to the national film board, what films are given to private film organizations, and who are the private film organizations that get these films. If this is indeed the case, it seems to me that it is an extremely serious situation so far as the national film board and staff are concerned.

In accordance with the policy announced in the house some time ago, employees in government departments and agencies handling classified material are examined for security. Earlier this year the national film board was included among those departments in connection with the production and processing of service films containing classified material. That examination for security is still being proceeded with.

Supply-National Defence

I do not think the minister has really answered the question, Mr. Chairman. Am I to take it that it is correct that the Department of National Defence refuses, for security reasons, to place certain filming in the hands of the national film board? Is that correct?

That is correct; until the film board, like any other agency, private or public, has had its employees screened for security, we will not place with it classified material for reproduction or processing.

I know that this film board is not in the minister's department, but I should certainly think that whatever minister has that department should forthwith see that these people are properly screened so that that department of government would not be cut off, for security reasons, from making films for the defence forces. It seems to me that that is a most anomalous situation.
I can assure the hon. member that the minister has that matter in hand.
What type of film would be made that could raise any question about the affiliations of any member of the film board?
Films that have to do with secret processes, films that have to do with research, new weapons, new training methods and so on, some of which may originate in Canada and some in other countries.

Can the minister tell us what has been the cost in the past year of films for the national defence forces? I should also like to know what the cost for advertising has been, and particularly what the cost of advertising has been for the recruiting campaign which has been carried on during the past year.

The cost of recruiting advertising for the last year was: for the navy, $236,246; for the army, $324,573; and for the air force, $282,931. The amount spent on films would partly be included in those figures, because some of the films were used for recruiting purposes. But the services use films now to a great extent in training work. Such films of course do not enter into recruiting expenses at all. The total amount spent on training equipment and films for 1948-49 is $238,737, of which a very small proportion would be for films.
Has the minister the figures broken down to show how much this recruiting advertising works out at per man recruited? It works out in the total, I can see, to about $700,000 or a little better.

It works out at about $65 per man. We have also of course again compared


that figure with recruiting expenses in other campaigns and other countries; and I find that it is not out of line.
Does that include the people recruited in the reserve forces?
Just for the active forces.
For the active forces only?

I am glad the hon. member corrected me because at the same time we have recruited a larger number as well for the reserve force. Related to the active force recruits it works out at something like $65 a man. Related to the two, active and reserve, it works out at much less than half that.

I was startled by the minister's statement that certain films were not being entrusted to the employees of the national film board but were being entrusted to employees of commercial firms. What screening has been done in regard to these particular commercial firms' employees? If, as appears on the face of it, the minister is prepared to entrust these films to commercial people but is not prepared to entrust them to employees of the national film board, I should like to have some explanation. I may be mistaken in my understanding. It does not seem logical to me.

I do not suggest for a second that it is logical, but apparently it was practical because these film companies who were charged with the job of doing larger processing work had small processing units, or relatively small processing units, that were not engaged in the same type of creative activity as the film board, and therefore it made it easier to screen their particular employees; I am told that the difficulty in connection with the film board, when this was discovered as it was this year, when the question of using agencies for processing films came up, was that with the number of employees concerned with the film board it would take some time to screen them.

I am to understand that the employees of these particular commercial firms have been screened in connection with the work they have to do for the Department of National Defence, whereas the employees of the national film board have not been so screened.
That is right.

When the matter was up before, I asked the minister who these companies were who are now working on what might be called secret films or films which might require security personnel for their production. Perhaps he forgot to reply and I did not remind him immediately.
Crawley, an Ottawa firm, is one; and another, subject to confirmation, is the Associated Screen News.

I think the remark of the Minister of National Defence on this subject is the most telling kind of indictment of a government agency that we have ever heard from the lips of a government minister or a member for a long time, directed, in this case, to the national film board. It will come as a shock to many Canadians to be told that the Department of National Defence did not find itself in the position to entrust to the national film board the making of films for the purpose of the Department of National Defence because the employees of that government agency could not be entrusted with it on account of doubts as to their trustworthiness on security grounds.
From our point of view-

It is not so many years ago, Mr. Chairman, that there was strong criticism levelled at the national film board because one Freda Linton, a notorious communist, had been a very active and prominent member of the staff of the national film board. I think most of us in this house had hoped that after that unhappy experience steps had been taken by those responsible in the government and in the national film board for directing affairs of the board to see that that type of employee was eliminated from the national film board. We are told tonight by the minister that the Department of National Defence was not prepared to entrust the making of films for the use of the department to the national film board because of lack of screening of employees of that board. I do urge upon the minister-he has indicated it is not his department-and upon the government that no time should be lost in carrying out such an effective screening of the national film board as will qualify that board to make films of the kind sought by the Department of National Defence and do similar duties for the government of Canada as may be required.
When did the Department of National Defence start the policy of not employing the national film board to make these films?

The policy was not started from any specific date. From our point of view it was not a question of doubt, but rather the fact that the screening which was necessary in dealing with processing and productions of this kind had not been completed. It has not yet been completed.

I do not think that answers the question. I presume at one time the department did have films of this nature taken
Supply-National Defence by the national film board, and then at some period it ceased to have this done because of security reasons. What I wanted was the date that they ceased to entrust this work to the national film board.

Subject to correction, the department did not stop entrusting any particular class of work to the national film board. During the war this kind of thing was done to a considerable degree by other agencies, and some of it was done within the department itself. We have not given work of a restricted nature to the national film board because their screening has not been completed.

Mr. Chairman, I think that there should be a clarification of the position in regard to the subject, because it is one that goes beyond the national film board. When the minister's attention was drawn to the article in the Financial Post he indicated that the report was correct, that certain specified films are not being entrusted to the national film board because of the fact that they are being screened. We know what that means. It means that they are being screened for possible communists in the organization. That is the reason for the screening. That was announced in this house. The minister has explained to us that this is in keeping with the policy that was announced in the house. The policy in regard to the screening of the departments of government was one that was announced comparatively recently; whereas the statement made by the minister just now is to the effect that these outside agencies were employed for the purpose of making films, and that that practice has not been discontinued. These two statements do not go side by side. They do not hit each other. Either there has been a discontinuance of the use of the national film board for certain specified purposes because of the fact that they are being screened, or there has not. If there has been, then it is proper to ask when that action was taken, and when the activities of the film board in that respect were suspended.

I am afraid that the leader of the opposition and the hon. member who spoke before are going beyond the information I now have. My information is that there was no discontinuance, because this job was not done by the film board before; but that when the question came up of its being undertaken by the film board it became necessary from our point of view to have the film board regarded as an agency of the government which must be screened, and that process is still going on.

When did it start?

Supply-National Defence
My recollection is that it would be in May, 1949.
Perhaps we could get at this matter from another direction. I wonder whether the minister knows who screened these other people, Crawley and the Associated Screen News, and when that was done?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried?
No, I want an answer.

I would have to get that information for the hon. member. I was not there myself, I can assure him. I know of only one agency in the government service that does this screening, and that is the R.C.M.P. I cannot say it was the R.C.M.P., because I have not seen their reports. I would assume however that it was they, because it is the only agency I know of that does this sort of thing. These reports would be dealt with by the appropriate officials who, when satisfied, would proceed to place the business. The hon. member may take it that it was the R.C.M.P.

In addition to that, it seems to me the minister or some of his officials must have the date when these others were screened by the R.C.M.P., and when the Department of National Defence was assured that it was all right to have them make these secret films. I think if we got that date it might tie in as being the same date they ceased using the national film board. Will the minister get that information?
Perhaps we had better pass on to the next question while I try to get the information on this one.

This is a matter which in my opinion the minister will have to clarify tonight. We have members of the press in the gallery, and it would appear rather ridiculous if the public were to read in tomorrow's press, particularly after all the emphasis we have been putting on communism in the debate during the last few days on external affairs, that we have a department of government with an appropriation in the estimates of some $2 million that cannot be trusted to do some work for the Department of National Defence.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is in the house, and I believe the national film board comes under his jurisdiction. It is strange that employees who are taken on by the civil service, who have written the examinations and whose character and background have been checked, should be in question. Their honesty and integrity so far as Canada is concerned are checked before they are actually hired.


It is most important that this matter should not be let drop tonight. I should not like the people whom I represent to think that I sat here and passed an estimate for national defence while in a state of mind in which I was wondering what we are going to defend, or who was going to defend what. Is it a fact that we have a huge branch of government entrusted with practically all publicity of a visual nature which goes out throughout the country, and into other countries, but which the Department of National Defence cannot trust to make films for them?
Surely this is within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who is responsible for that department. It it is suspect, he should know something about it. If it is not, then he should clarify the matter tonight in the house so that the press may have a clear picture to give to the people of Canada tomorrow.
I cannot understand how a minister can tell the house that we cannot trust a branch the employees of which must have been carefully screened before they were hired, and still can go out to private agencies in this city. Apparently he knows very little about how they were screened and who vouched for them. Yet he cannot trust his own branch. Surely the matter requires clarification. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply presides over the national film board. I have always had considerable respect for the board, and I suggest he should have something to say tonight about it.

This seems to me an amazing situation. I would ask the minister if it is the intention to give this work to the film board as soon as this screening has been completed, and how long he expects such screening to take.

We would be glad to give the work, such as it is-and it does not amount to much-to any agency that can satisfy the requirements laid down by the government with respect to the screening of its employees. From the review I have made of the file while the debate has been going on, I would suggest there has not been any sharp, hard-and-fast decision of the kind that might be imagined. As we moved from the period of war to the post-war period we naturally had many films, and then we began to produce some new ones. Most of these were not of a restricted or classified nature. Some of them were done by the film board and some by other agencies.
It was only with the announcement of the government's policy with regard to the screening of agencies of the government and employees of the government, and the general tightening of security regulations which.

took place more than a year ago, and which have gradually been overtaken and overhauled, that such questions as dealing with films which might be classified as confidential-and that does not mean in the top secret class-came up for consideration.
When that arose, the question also arose as to the possibility of dealing with the film board in sections so as to facilitate the speed of screening. Apparently there was some difficulty about that, and there was a good deal of correspondence as to how it should be handled. During such time, and until the screening is completed, there has not been any classified material handled by the film board. That is the position.
I am sure the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will say that the screening is being proceeded with, and as soon as it is completed satisfactorily the film board will deal with films of a restricted nature.

With ail due respect, I do not think the statement the minister has just made has helped his previous statement one bit. The fact remains

and it is as bald as any fact can be-that last May, because they were not prepared to entrust the making of these films to the national film board on account of security doubts in reference to the film board, the Department of National Defence discontinued the making of films through that source, and turned to some private concern.
That was six months ago. This is November. How far has the screening process gone? The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is in the house tonight, and it is under his department that the film board falls. In the intervening six months, the minister must have become aware that the Department of National Defence were withdrawing that work from the national film board. Has he taken steps to press forward with the work of reviewing the records in the film board, to make sure that those doubts are removed, and that all security problems have been resolved within the board?
This is a serious matter. I have already referred to the very serious question raised in times past about certain individuals in the board. I mentioned Freda Linton. Surely that is one place where this screening should have started. The minister has indicated that this started six months ago and I think the committee is entitled to know from the minister of reconstruction what progress has been made during that time in screening personnel in the national film board. The committee should be told if after that time it is
Supply-National Defence considered that the national film board is now in position to justify on security grounds the making of films for the Department of National Defence.

My estimates are not before the committee, but when they are I shall be glad to discuss the affairs of the film board. Certain questions have been asked as to whether steps are being taken to satisfy the Department of National Defence and any other department that deals with the national film board as to its security. I should say that the mere fact that the Department of National Defence asks for a screening does not imply that that department is or is not satisfied with the security which it considers should prevail in the film board.
It is quite automatic.

The department is simply asking that the employees be classified. We have asked the R.C.M.P. to press forward. In reply to the specific question as to whether or not we are pressing forward, the answer is yes. We have urged the authorities to press forward as quickly as possible. As hon. members will understand, it is not easy to screen people on a relatively large scale. There is not information in the R.C.M.P. files on everybody; perhaps that is a good thing and perhaps it is not. I am sure the Minister of Justice would have more to say about this subject. But again in reply to the question as to whether we are pressing the matter, the answer is yes.

When I asked the minister a little while ago about screening I thought his ans-wer would refer to the R.C.M.P., but there is another thought in my mind. During the war we had a reasonably good intelligence corps, and I suppose we have a reasonably good one now. I am wondering if it was because of the recommendation of that intelligence corps that it was decided it was better not to have these films made by the national film board.
I know that some people may think that the defence intelligence should not be digging into such matters, but personally I take the reverse point of view. As far as I am concerned, if the Department of National Defence thought that the national film board were not the proper people from the security point of view to make their films I would commend them for their intestinal fortitude in standing up to what is described in the Financial Post article as a virtual monopoly as far as government film business is concerned. What part did the national defence intelligence service play in this?
