Supply-National Defence

As the minister of reconstruction said, it was not a case of having found out anything; it was simply a case of having a job undertaken by the R.C.M.P. and pressed forward as quickly as possible. When a report is received from the R.C.M.P. or from the Department of Justice with regard to the security of any person in a "vulnerable" department, it is examined by the department concerned. In the case of the Department of National Defence, the examination in the first instance would be by the intelligence officers.
I can assure my hon. friend that they are just as strict and stern about such matters as he would wish them to be. In fact they sometimes advise me in ways which he himself has felt might be a little excessive.
When reports are received from the Department of Justice they are examined by the directors of intelligence of each service, with reference in the case of special instructions and directives in difficult cases to the joint intelligence committee or the joint intelligence board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think possibly I should say a few words of explanation. This matter came to my attention when I was Secretary of State for External Affairs. Hon. members will realize that we have a number of exchanges with other governments and there are different classifications of the material we send out and receive. The question arose as to what precautions we were taking to secure secrecy in such matters as might be considered secret or confidential, and there are various classifications. At that time the matter was considered carefully and it is still being considered carefully.
At times there have been what might be considered as leakages, not in connection with external affairs but in connection with our own domestic matters. Sometimes we read in the newspapers speculative stories that come near to what has been discussed in secret cabinet meetings. Then there are leakages of information in the sense that something sometimes becomes public before the agreed time when it was to become public. Because of that and to satisfy ourselves and those from whom we received and to whom we sent material it was felt that we should have a system that we could look upon as being secure.
When we went into the matter we came to the conclusion that this security should extend, not only to the Department of External Affairs and the Prime Minister's office but to the other departments to which documents of these various classifications were sent. It was felt that all those who were
[Mr. Harkness.l

to have access to this material should be vouched for by the deputy head of the department.
The statement is made that the screening is done by the R.C.M.P. The R.C.M.P. does not make any decision about any individual. The R.CM.P. obtains a factual report and communicates it to the responsible deputy head of the department where the man is employed. Then the deputy head or the minister of that department must take the responsibility of saying whether or not that civil servant can be entrusted with classified material. That system has been extended to the Department of National Defence as it has to other departments that have access to material thus classified. Until the responsible head of a branch of government is prepared to say that he takes the responsibility for having secret documents entrusted to so-and-so, it is not done; and that process has not been completed with respect to the film board.
Hon. members will realize that we have to be careful. We do not want to do anything unfair relative to any individual. This is not a snooping process to undermine the character of anyone. It is being done in order to place the responsible head of each department in a position where he personally can vouch for all those who have access to the confidential material coming into his department. The R.C.M.P. were very reluctant even to go about securing the information, and it was found necessary to say to them, "Well, you will not have to make the decision. You just get a factual report and submit it to the permanent head of the department concerned. He will make the decision as to whether from that factual report he is satisfied that he can vouch for the person concerned." Not a large number of the personnel of the R.C.M.P. are engaged on that work, because it is rather disagreeable to anyone to have it said that he is being investigated. So it is being proceeded with in a discreet manner that will enable a responsible official of the mounted police to say, "This is all we can find out about this man." Then the responsible head of the department has to say whether that is enough for him to take the responsibility of entrusting that man with classified material. That is being done in connection with all those who in the normal course of the exercise of their functions would have access to confidential material.

In view of the remarks of the Prime Minister I think it would be appropriate for us to be told if there are any

other departments which at the present time are having outside agencies do the work they ordinarily would do because any branch of those departments is being screened in this way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know of any other; but I do know that it is not everyone in my own office, as it is not everyone in the Department of External Affairs, to whom confidential material is entrusted. It is to those who have been screened, those for whom the head of the department feels he can take the responsibility of saying that it is not unfair to those who look to us to maintain proper security that the documents be entrusted.

In reply to the leader of the opposition I think it should be made clear, too, that there has been no switch from the film board to the Crawley firm or to Associated Screen News. When the work of postwar organization was being proceeded with it was felt at a certain stage that the film board came within the class of government agencies which should be screened, and that work is being proceeded with. Mind you, the Department of National Defence, the Department of External Affairs and all government agencies concerned with restricted material are screened in this way.

I could not help overhearing one hon. member remark that this was making a mountain out of a molehill. It is not. This is a most unusual situation. The Minister of National Defence has just explained that there has been no withdrawal of work on this particular type of film from the national film board but that it is a continuation of work which was being done by two outside firms whose names he has mentioned, who are well known and highly reputable business concerns. If that is the case it is difficult to understand how this situation is related to the screening process which was undertaken a year ago, and which the minister has already given as the reason for the fact that the national film board is not doing this particular task.
Again, it does seem this is the sort of thing on which we should have a perfectly clear understanding. Either this work is not being done by the national film board because the national film board is being screened, or that is not the case. The last explanation given by the minister is simply to the effect that work is still being done which at an earlier date was entrusted to these two outside agencies. I think we should know whether or not some action has been taken in relation to this screening.
Supply-National Defence

Both statements are correct, and they are not irreconcilable. The work is not being done by the national film board because it is being screened, and the work is continuing to be done by outside agencies which have been screened. The amount of work in question is very small indeed, which is probably one reason why the matter did not come to the fore earlier.

That is one reason why this is a subject which should be thoroughly discussed while these estimates are before the committee. It will be recalled that one of the recommendations of the Mainguy report was that greater use be made of the national film board for the purpose of films to be used in the naval service. Every hon. member of this committee remembers the ancient Chinese adage that one picture tells a more complete story than a thousand words. That is perhaps even more true in the case of the moving picture than the still picture. Not only from the point of view of entertainment and recreation but from the point of view of instruction the moving picture film is of immense value. If the national film board is not being called in, or this work done by outside agencies has reached any substantial proportions, then I should say very definitely that here is one detail in connection with our national defence preparations which is not being properly carried out. There is no way by which many of the details of instruction can be better brought to the personnel of the army, the navy or the air force than by motion pictures, particularly in the case of parts, equipment and things of that kind and the placing of them together. By means of slow-motion pictures a very clear explanation can be given of all the details.
I do think this should not be left in the vague position it is in at the present time, because it raises another question in the mind of everyone here. If the fact that the national film board is being screened is the reason why it is not being entrusted with the taking of pictures which the minister has stated are not top secret but are at the secret level, then how can he explain the fact that other agencies of government which also are being screened nevertheless are carrying on their normal activities? As far as this committee is aware no other branch of any other department has been withdrawn from its ordinary functions, because of being screened, as is the case with the national film board. Either there must be some special reason in this case, or this whole system of screening may well create difficulties in different departments which had not been anticipated at the time it was announced.

Supply-National Defence
I would point out, as the Prime Minister said, that in his department as in every other department naturally there are certain people who would be particularly designated to carry out certain highly secret or important discussions. It would seem that it would not be a very difficult thing to designate a limited number of employees of the national film board to carry out this particular type of work, in any case where there is some measure of secrecy. I think the explanation just does not hold water, and we should know what the facts really are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I believe the hon. leader of the opposition is under a misapprehension. We are told by our security committee that it will be necessary to have all those employed by the film board who could possibly have access to confidential material screened, before it will be proper to entrust that board with the preparation of classified material. Because it is felt that it would be the proper thing to have all this work or as much of it as possible done by the government agency, this screening is undertaken. It is intended to have the film board certified to be in a position, or have them get into a position, where the classified material can be entrusted to them.

This seems to me to raise a serious question, when one department of the government cannot be trusted to do certain work and private firms can be trusted. I should like to know what steps the government has taken to screen those private firms that are doing this secret work. The employees of those companies are not the employees of the government, and the government has no control over them. If this work is of such a nature that the film board cannot be entrusted with it, I should like to know how these private firms can be trusted and what screening of these companies has been done which gives the government the confidence that these firms can carry out the work without any danger to our security.

I can answer that question in a way that will help to make this clear. During the war the national film board had a great deal of work to do in connection with war information. As hon. members know, it produced all sorts of films of an informational character. The type of film that we are talking about here, the restricted or secret film, was handed to other agencies than the film board, not for reasons of security but for reasons of convenience at that stage. That situation still continues. The film board still does the great bulk of the work for all government agencies, including the armed forces, work of a training character, an informational character and publicity character.

With regard to this relatively small restricted class of material, the arrangements which existed during the war are being continued, pending the clearing of the employees of the film board for security.
The minister has not yet answered my question as to the method used by the government in screening the employees of the private firms. How do you screen the employees of the private firm?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The answer is that the firm takes the responsibility for certifying that secrecy will be observed, whilst in the government department a deputy head takes the responsibility for certifying that so-and-so, whom he knows personally, is well enough known to him that he does not have to be screened. There are others about whom the deputy head has not sufficient knowledge to take the responsibility of certifying to us that he can be entrusted with confidential documents. With respect to those people, we asked to have a report made by an investigator of the R.C.M.P. and submitted to the deputy head. On that report the deputy head can say whether or not he will take the responsibility of vouching for that member of his staff.

If I understand the Prime Minister correctly, his remarks have given us a considerably different picture. The Minister of National Defence told us that the film board people were being screened, and that he would receive information about the employees of the private firms who were also being screened by the R.C.M.P. If I understand the Prime Minister correctly the R.C.M.P. did not do any screening at all; they merely got information about certain people-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what we call "screening".

Then, that information was turned over to the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Public Works or whoever it may be. It is then up to that minister and his officials to make a decision as to whether or not those people should be entrusted with any secret work. If that is the situation, then so far as I can see the R.C.M.P. must have turned in to the Department of National Defence information in connection with certain persons in the film board, and as a result of that information the defence department people said, "No, we will not have those people do any secret pictures for us." That is the situation as I see it at the moment. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is only partially correct. It is not as a result of having seen reports that were unfavourable; it is due to

the fact that enough reports have not been seen to say that the whole board is certified for security purposes. In the story the hon. member read from the Financial Post, you have an example of the fact that there is leakage. It was not intended to publish this, and I do not think it is in the public interest that it should be published and discussed here. It is something that we would have preferred not to see published, but it has leaked out. How, we do not know. Where the newspaperman got his informaion, we do not know. We are inclined to believe he did not get it from the officials of the R.C.M.P.

Would the Prime Minister not agree with me that this is the sort of information that members of parliament should be given, if there exists a department of this government to which another department is not willing to entrust secret work? It seems to me it is a matter which calls for some parliamentary discussion. I can hardly see the Prime Minister's point that matters of this sort should be kept from us, and of course, generally speaking, from the people of Canada.
If it happened to be such a matter as perhaps should not be made public, then I would suggest once more that the committee for which we have been pressing would have been the proper place to give that information.

We seem to be getting away from these commercial firms. It would banish some confusion and certainly in my own mind if the minister would say whether, in putting the work in the hands of these commercial firms, there was any other consideration except that of secrecy?
I believe, sir, at the time the work was first put there, it was put there because this was work-
I am not speaking of wartime when everyone was very busy.
Since then the work has been put there because we were continuing to follow the patterns established during the war.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
A few moments ago the Prime Minister expressed the view that the government would have preferred not to have this matter discussed and publicized in this way, but he admitted it is now out in the full view of the public. It seems to me that the matter becomes worse as the discussion continues. Is the Prime Minister willing to leave it to the press now to say that the government is prepared to accept the word of the heads of private film organizations that there is no danger to security in employing them, but is not prepared to trust its own film board? It boils down to that, as the matter now stands.
Supply-National Defence

No, that is not the situation. It is known that these private firms have been doing work of that character for a good many years. There has been no suggestion that absolute secrecy was not being observed. The question arose as to whether the work should not be taken away from them and all be given to the film board. The decision was that that would not be done until the minister responsible for the film board had had reports that satisfied him that for security purposes we could vouch for the film board.

I think, Mr. Chairman, you will see some of the difficulties which the minister experiences with this policy of unification, because I now want to discuss quite a different subject, that of the air force.

Before the hon. member passes on to that subject, may I just add a word. I am saying that I regret that this matter has become public, not because it is embarrassing to the government but because I think it is unfortunate that there should be any impression-and there will be such an impression-that those who are in the employ of the board are under a cloud. I think it is unfortunate that they should be under a cloud. We were endeavouring to proceed in such a manner as to obtain certification without anyone going under a cloud. This premature publicity, before we are in a position to make a positive statement that each one has been examined and that we are prepared to vouch for each one, is unfortunate; it is unfortunate that any cloud should be resting on the group.

Until the Prime Minister made his statement, I thought I understood the situation. The Prime Minister now says that work is given to firms where assurance is given that secrecy will be maintained. In other words, screening is not required. But earlier the Minister of National Defence said that this work is given to firms whose employees have already been screened. Can we say definitely that firms that are doing the work today have screened their employees? The Minister of National Defence said that they had; the Prime Minister says no; that they only required an assurance.

No, I do not say that they have not been screened; I say that I do not know. I say that, as far as I was concerned, that work was continued because it had been done during the period of the war and no untoward incidents that I know of had happened at that time. I cannot say that every individual employed by those firms has been screened. As far as I know, we were relying on the firm and not upon a decision of our own; whilst with respect to the film board,

Supply-National Defence we will look to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to say to us that he has satisfied himself that we can vouch, to those from whom we get and to whom we supply secret material, that all those having access to it can be trusted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Prime Minister said that there is no evidence that they know of any untoward incident-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -on the part of employees of the private firms.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Nor of the film board.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the question I wanted to ask.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Nor of the film board.

Is the Prime Minister
through?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I apologize for having broken in, but I thought it was only fair to these employees of the film board that f should endeavour to put the situation as right as it can be put at this moment.

Will the Prime Minister say why, all of a sudden, the government has ceased to trust the employees of the film board? He says that nothing has come out, that nothing has been divulged. Why do they suddenly not trust those employees?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Up to the present time they have never done any of this confidential work. The question arose as to whether they should not be required to do it instead of our continuing to have it done by the firms which had been doing it. Before coming to that conclusion, we want the minister responsible to say to us that he has satisfied himself that we can vouch, to those who send us confidential material and to whom we supply confidential material, that all the members of the film board can be trusted with confidential material. That investigation has not yet been proceeded with to the extent that our colleague is prepared to take that responsibility to us, and we are therefore not prepared to take it with those with whom we are associated in exchanging this confidential material.

I am obliged to change the subject, and I think the Prime Minister will agree that we have discussed long enough the one to which our attention has just been directed.
Under section 97 of the white paper, the strengths of the reserve forces are given, and the figure of 3,086 is given for the air force. I was going to ask the minister

whether those 3,086 personnel are divided between the ten squadrons of the air force auxiliary and the radar units of the air force auxiliary as shown under section 117.

Yes, plus a certain number of air force reserve called up to receive pay on a full-time basis. This would permit us to consider the figure of 3,086 on precisely the same basis as the corresponding figures for the numbers of naval reserve divisions or for the army reserves effective.
Mt. Pearkes: Can the minister give a breakdown of that 3,086, as to how many are in those air squadrons, how many are in the radar unit, how many of those are called up from this general reserve and also how many are flying personnel and how many are ground crew?

That is a breakdown into categories that are complex, and I shall have to get the information for the hon. member. The great majority are in the ten squadrons. There are some 250 in the radar unit, and a relatively small proportion are in the reserves that are called up. I can give the hon. gentleman the exact figures and also the division between air and ground crew.
Thank you. Are those reserves which are called up serving with the auxiliary squadron?
Yes.
They are not a separate branch?
No.

Then when we come to the active air force, the figures given are 16,356. Can the minister give a breakdown of that figure showing how many are flying personnel, how many are ground personnel and how many are administrative personnel not taking part in flying operations?
I have that breakdown. I can give it to the hon. gentleman later.

I am anxious to get that information because I think it will show, far more clearly than the mere total numbers, the number of flying personnel that we have. That is the point I want to get at.
From what the minister has just told us, the reserve air force is not a reserve at all, except that it is allocated to auxiliary fighter units. What organization is there for replacement of flying personnel in the active units should hostilities break out and operations

take place, and should it be necessary-as it would be if there were operations-to replace a large number of the flying personnel?

The first source of replacements-they really would not be replacements, they would be additions to the air force flying personnel-would come from auxiliary units themselves. Then there are a number of classifications of air force reserves, six in number. No great effort has been made to recruit these up to large strengths, because they are all available in the event of an emergency, and no great advantage would be gained in taking on the extra paper work to keep in touch with them. But included among them, of course, are the members who served in the R.C.A.F. or R.A.F. from Canada during the war, in the course of which some 71,000 air crew of Canadian origin were trained. A number of them are still available, and with retraining would be available.
Then in the universities at the present time we have some 679 in training. It is hoped that that number will be increased with the increase of training facilities. This represents a small proportion of what would be needed in the event of war, but we are proceeding with the training as rapidly as possible.
In connection with the figure of 3,086 for the air force auxiliary, I might mention again the figure I gave today from a return in the United Kingdom where the corresponding number, at the 29th of September, was 5,350; so that in proportion our figure is measuring up rather well; but it is still far short of what we would need.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that from what the minister has said I had ample justification for being concerned as to where the replacements for the active air force flying personnel would come from. It was suggested by the minister just now that the first line would be to deplete-he did not use the word "deplete"-or to draw from the auxiliary squadrons.
"Draw through", I think, would be a better term.

Draw through the auxiliary squadrons. I presume that would be drawing untrained people because I do not know where they exist now except that they are the ex-R.C.A.F. personnel and ex-R.A.F. personnel who are in Canada. These people are getting on in years, and that is not creating an organization. From what the minister has said I see no organization where he has any men in training coming up as a big reserve of trained men, except those 600 from the universities.
Supply-National Defence
On that again we have doubled within one year the number in the auxiliary and the number in the university or training plans.
I am glad to hear the word "doubled". I hope that he will double it again very quickly because I think it is the Achilles heel of the defence force.

It is certainly a very important factor, and again it is one which depends on the use of resources. As the hon. member knows, it costs a great deal of money to train air crew, and they are available for an effective service life of limited duration. We are pressing on with another category which I should mention, and which I omitted before, namely, men training for short service commissions; that is, men who are taken on to the air force regular strength, with educational standards generally equivalent to senior matriculation. They are given a period of service of five years. Then they are eligible, if they are selected, for continuation in permanent commissions, but that method of augmenting air crew has been extended during the last two years-
Where would these men be shown? Under the 16,000?
Yes, under the 16,000.
So the 16,000 active force includes a lot of people who are temporary.

Who are in training for air crew but are not there temporarily in the sense that it is just for a matter of weeks, but who have joined on for periods of five years in order to provide a larger number of air crew for the period of active flying life. They are part of the active forces.

They are in reserve outside. They can hardly be considered as replacements. The minister will be able to get me a breakdown of this figure, showing how many are flying personnel and how many are ground crews.
Oh, yes.

Regarding radar units, which the minister spoke about, can he tell us the policy regarding these radar units? Are they all going to be stationed in the north, or are they all going to be stationed around industrial centres, or are they going to be organized and are they all going to be manned by the R.C.A.F., or will some be manned by the army in co-operation with perhaps antiaircraft units, and some with the navy? What is going to be the organization? Is there going to be a special corps set up, a radar corps, or what?

Supply-National Defence
Send it to Russia. They want to know all these things.

As I said in the house the other night, there is no intention on the part of the department or the government at this time to set up anything of the nature of a radar screen or grid that would effectively cover Canada as Britain or Germany was covered by radar during the war. That is quite beyond the resources of Canada. Even the most effective radar screen is successful only in detecting a certain proportion of the enemy planes. Then there is required a communications network, backed by interceptor planes to bring them down. Canada is so big that it is not susceptible of defence in that way, and it is no part of our present plan to defend it in that way. If we were to set about defending it in that way we would be spending so great a proportion of our national income on static defence that we would not have any money left for any other purpose whatever in the way of defence, and consequently that is not the idea.
What we plan to do is to have a number of radar stations located at various points, which are regarded as useful from the point of view of intercepting any enemy on a likely course, and which are regarded as useful also from the point of view of affording protection to a limited area. At the beginning that area will be very limited; but we hope that means may be forthcoming to extend it. This work will be done by permanent forces, the air force at the more isolated centres, supplemented by air force reserve units such as the first one established at Montreal, which is making very good progress under the really first-class leadership of Squadron Leader Patrick. It was that unit which took part in the Exercise Metropolis, when some two or three hundred members of the regular and auxiliary air forces brought mobile equipment to New York and assisted in the detection and interception of aircraft there.
The radar unit in Montreal we hope will be followed soon by one in Toronto and in other principal centres where we can draw upon officers and men with either air force or radar experience, or having particular interests in that field of work through being engaged in the electronics or electrical industry.

I wish again to make an appeal on behalf of the personnel of the reserve forces and the officers and instructors of the cadet corps across Canada in connection with their pay being subject to income tax. The minister knows this matter has been discussed on other occasions, and he mentioned this afternoon that it was under consideration.


I am wondering who is holding it up, because it has been under consideration for several years. I feel sure the minister is not, but it must be either the Minister of National Revenue or the head of some other department. This is a grave injustice to these personnel. I know from personal experience, when I had something to do with sea cadets during the war, that while I did not receive pay at that time the amount I was called upon to spend to keep the thing going was far more than anything I would have received in the form of pay. I know that is the position today, and it is a grave injustice being forced upon this personnel who are devoting their time, in addition to their other regular activities, to the defence forces of Canada. There should not be any further delay in considering this matter in favour of those chaps who in some cases are giving all their spare time toward improving the defence forces of this country. Then these additions are made to their incomes, and they are taxed on it. In my opinion this is most unfair.

I appreciate what the hon. member has said. What is holding it up is the provision in the Income Tax Act. What is needed is a formula whereby the pay of reserve and cadet officers shall not be considered as income. If the hon. member can invent that he will have solved the problem.

I would like to suggest a formula to correct this situation. I agree entirely with what has been said by the hon. member for Wentworth. We heard the other day, from the Minister of Finance, a formula through which we are going to beautify Ottawa. You just take 80 per cent from 60 per cent and add 4 per cent, and find out how old your mother-in-law is, and then 'phone for Einstein-and you have it. I am entirely in accord with what the hon. member has said, and it is high time the Minister of National Revenue, or whoever is responsible, gave us some action in this matter.
Carried.

For the benefit of some hon. members who are calling "carried" let me say I have eight more questions jotted down, so they might as well save their breath.
My first question has to do with the navy. Under the heading in the details which deals with equipment and things of that nature there is an item of $26 million. How much of that is for ship construction? The item also includes the purchase of trucks and other types of equipment.

It is broken down as follows:

Is this $6 million for ship construction and acquisition chiefly for the three new subchasers being built? Would a portion of their cost come under this, or is it for other than that?

This afternoon and last Friday we had a general discussion as to the proportion of forces in what I would call actual fighting units as compared with those in command and administrative posts. In that connection, and to get down to something more definite, can the minister tell us how much of the money in these appropriations is for the reserve brigade group (army) and how much is for the operational squadrons of the air force, so far as the air force is concerned?

There is no possibility of making any such breakdown without going through every item of defence expenditures from start to finish, because the expenses of headquarters staffs, R.C.E.M.E. workshops, ordnance corps, ordnance corps stores and so on are not kept in books that relate to the ultimate consumer. The portions of the overhead and the like are not related in that way. There is no way of giving that information from our figures.

If the minister cannot give us a breakdown along that line, could he tell us where the shortages of manpower in respect of the establishments he hopes to have in a reasonably short space of time are to be found? In other words, are those shortages in the army, in the reserve brigade group or at headquarters staff, or are they in the army service corps supply units, or where are they?
Supply-National Defence And, so far as the air force is concerned, are those shortages of manpower in the establishment of operational squadrons or in some of the administrative positions?

They are scattered through. The greatest shortages proportionately are in the occupational groups requiring the highest educational standings, senior matriculation and the like. I think that applies to both the army and the air force. As I say, the navy is up to strength in other ranks personnel. It is divided between various units. As the various units are filled up the opportunity of joining those is not extended to men applying for recruitment; if they want to join the army their choice is limited.
The proportions of the brigade group left to be filled up is made up in part of men who are already in the training stream in the various corps schools and who will be posted to units in the brigade group so that the shortage there should be filled relatively speedily.
Do I understand that when the present recruits whom you have taken in and who are now undergoing training are posted out the brigade group will be pretty well up to strength?
To about 70 or 75 per cent, something of that character.

From the details I notice that the vote for the reserve army is approximately $200,000 more this year than it was last year. The minister told us earlier that they hoped to get a considerable increase in the reserve forces and that a considerable increase had already been secured for last year and he hoped it would be increased still further. I am wondering how that considerable increase in the numbers in the reserve army is going to be looked after when there is only an increase of $200,000 in the vote. Did the minister and the department estimate that there would not be much of an increase and therefore did not budget for any more than $200,000 extra?

We hoped for a large increase and the increase has been considerable. If the money available for the reserve forces as set out here is inadequate and there is money available in other votes, it is possible by application to the treasury board to secure an allocation to meet the additional cost. The reserve force vote last year was larger than was required and that is why it is only $200,000 larger this year.

The details on page 198 show the biggest reduction to be in pay and allowances, from $6,300,000 in 1948-49 to $5,701,000

Supply-National Defence for the current year. That would seem to indicate that the department had estimated that the reserve army would be smaller this year.

It is exactly the reverse. The estimate for 1948-49 was larger than proved to be necessary and therefore it was not necessary to increase the estimate proportionately with the additional numbers and activity that we anticipated. Because we underspent on this item in 1948-49 it was possible and proper to put in the smaller increase which is here, but that is not on account of reduced activity.

I take it that, as far as last year was concerned, the number of people you thought would be in the reserve army and the amount of training you thought would be required was considerably less than had been estimated?
The cost was.
In other words, the recruiting scheme was comparatively less successful than you had budgeted or hoped for last year?

We have been trying to build up the army reserve steadily and have done everything possible to assure that. In consequence of the interest shown we hope we may be able to get an extra 10,000 men. Nevertheless, last year we enlisted 12,000 men in the army reserve.

I thank the minister for the explanation he has given. I thought it peculiar that he was budgeting for a smaller amount for pay and allowances and for the training of these reserve force soldiers. I notice that the item covering personnel supplies and services, which includes food supplies, is up approximately $10 million just for the army. The number in the army is not very much greater comparatively now than it was last year and I was wondering why this item should be so markedly or sharply increased?

The increase is largely due to the increase in the strength of the active army. As I pointed out, each extra man means an extra $2,600. I have the increase broken down into the various details. For one thing, the ration scale was increased, which increased the ration cost as from January, 1949.

The reason given by the minister would not seem to be applicable. This increase is for food, clothing and things of that sort and the total number in the

regular forces has increased by only a few thousand. That increased number certainly could not increase the vote from $8 million to $18 million. I think the explanation given by the minister must be wrong and that this increase is not due to the greater amount of food and clothing required.

I can give the hon. member the actual number of the increase which would be multiplied by $2,600, the cost per man. An additional $2,198,000 was required for food. An additional $743,000 is to be paid to the Department of Veterans Affairs for hospital services. The increased requirement for consumable dental stores reflecting using up of stocks from wartime surpluses, increased replacement of obsolescent dental equipment was $64,000. The increased requirement for purchase of cloth for manufacture of undress blue uniforms, purchase of Arctic clothing, bush type summer clothing, airborne stores, was $4,204,000. The increased provision for stoves and refrigerators for C.M.H.C. housing development, provision for Arctic barrack stores, provision for expendable materials, and lumber for ordnance depots, R.C.E.M.E. units and depots, provision for items of barrack and hospital stores, was $2,889,000. They provided the houses but we are to provide the stoves and refrigerators. Then there is an offsetting item reducing those additional items by $150,000, representing a reduction in laundry and dry cleaning. I think that accounts for the difference.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

On Monday we will take up the resolutions concerning the trans-Canada highway. I mention this because some time ago I consulted the leaders of the different parties, who gave me a list of the bills or resolutions they considered important, and this was one of them. So Monday morning at eleven o'clock we shall take up that resolution. The second item will be the second reading of Bill No. 149, respecting bankruptcy. I am told the motion for second reading will not involve much debate, and it is the intention to refer the bill to the committee on banking and commerce immediately second reading is given. Then we shall proceed with Bill No. 142, to amend the National Housing Act, which is in the committee stage. If we have time we shall take

up Bill No. 63, respecting the inspection ol fish and marine plants. That has been through committee, also.
